# IndyDevDan Expert Book — locked plan (Hermes orchestrates only)

## Goal
Become expert at IndyDevDan’s system: operate + teach-back + graded drills. HTML multi-volume site ~800–1000 pages (dense).

## Corpus Phase 1
- TAC 1–8 + AH 1–6 + MA 1–4 (local catalog)
- YT overlays last ~10 months: strict map-to-lesson / named-gap, 1–3 per lesson
- Phase 2: non-course YT later
- Phase 3: PAIC when access arrives

## Structure
Course-spine volumes + Current Practice YT overlays per lesson.
- Vol I TAC, Vol II AH, Vol III MA + synthesis
- Teaching model: Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name → Fail → Retrieval → Lab → Teach-back → Overlay

## Deliverable location
`/Users/kvnkishore/WebstormProjects/AgenticEngineer/IndyDevDan/book/`

## Labs
Course codebases only (not PiCanvas).

## Workers
- Claude Fable 5 (`--model fable` / `claude-fable-5`, `--effort max`): technical extract, codebase, accuracy, outdated flags
- Codex GPT 5.6 sol xhigh: teaching prose, weak-learner structure, HTML/UI craft
- Cross-review each other; stitch agent merges
- Hermes: prompts, dispatch, verify only — no book body by Hermes

{
  "lesson_key": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding",
  "title": "Hello Agentic Coding",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 1,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/hello-agentic-coding",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding/video/tac-1-hello-agentic-coding.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 1311,
    "duration_display": "21:51"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Stop Coding",
    "one_liner": "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code — hand the typing to agents and move your engineering cycles up the stack.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks career engineers to retire the skill that defined them. Dan spent over a decade at startups and large companies typing code by hand — mastering languages, syntax, algorithms, data structures — and says he misses it too. The tactic demands you trust that language models running in agentic loops on supercomputers are now vastly superior coders, and that clinging to hand-typing means you have no chance of keeping up. Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adopt new ones."
  },
  "mission": "Transform you into an engineer they can't replace — 'they' being your boss, the company, the industry, and AI itself. In a world where code is a commodity and your grandma or little brother can build an app with one prompt, you become irreplaceable the way engineers always have in technological revolutions: move up the stack. Become a commander of compute that builds systems that build systems, until your codebase runs itself.",
  "phase_model": {
    "phase1_ai_coding": "The generative-AI age's first phase: prompt-to-generate-code. Birth of vibe coders and the complete commoditization of code. You interact with the big three — context, model, prompt — to build faster than ever. Still foundational, no longer differentiating.",
    "phase2_agentic_coding": "Where real engineers strike back. A superset of AI coding: the big three plus tools — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tool calls inside an agentic coding tool. Engineers reallocate their cycles to planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures, and turn their codebases into increasingly self-operating machines."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-engineer",
      "name": "The Agentic Engineer — a new role",
      "plain_english": "A software engineer whose job is not writing code but building systems that can take actions the way an engineer would: branch, write, run, test, commit, report. Dan bought agenticengineer.com in 2023 betting this role would emerge; lesson 1 declares it now exists.",
      "dan_words": "\"Predicting that a new role of software engineering would emerge, defined by the ability to build systems that can take actions as we can. It's become clear this new role now exists.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'agentic engineer' is a rebrand of 'prompt engineer.' It isn't: the role is defined by system-building (embedding agents across the SDLC), not by writing clever one-off prompts."
    },
    {
      "id": "phase-one-vs-phase-two",
      "name": "Phase 1 (AI coding) vs Phase 2 (agentic coding)",
      "plain_english": "Phase 1 = using AI to generate code faster (context, model, prompt). Phase 2 = using AI to perform engineering work end-to-end (add tools). The lesson's entire arc is the delta between these two phases, demonstrated with two prompts in one README.",
      "dan_words": "\"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one. Here we saw the birth of VibeCoders and the complete commoditization of code... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.\"",
      "misconception": "That phase 2 replaces phase 1 knowledge. Agentic coding is a superset of AI coding — the big three are still there, always, even when you can't see them."
    },
    {
      "id": "stop-coding",
      "name": "Tactic #1: Stop Coding",
      "plain_english": "Stop typing code by hand. Not stop shipping code, not stop reading code — stop being the instrument that types it. Use the best tool for the job: agentic loops running powerful language models. Throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code is typed by hand.",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's end the debate right now. Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code, full stop.\"",
      "misconception": "Two opposite failure readings: (1) 'so we don't generate code anymore' — wrong, code is still a primary asset and you'll generate more than ever; (2) 'so I can stop understanding code' — wrong, code understanding is still critically important. What ends is hand-typing, and what replaces it is planning, reviewing, and closed-loop structures."
    },
    {
      "id": "commander-of-compute",
      "name": "Commander of Compute",
      "plain_english": "The identity shift of phase 2: your job is deciding where compute gets aimed and what systems it builds, not producing keystrokes. You don't just prompt to generate code — you direct compute to build systems that build systems.",
      "dan_words": "\"We move up the stack once again. We become a commander of compute... You take this compute and you use it to build systems that build systems.\"",
      "misconception": "That commanding compute means firing off more prompts manually. The command is structural — triggers, scripts, workflows that fire agents at the right time — not a human clicking faster."
    },
    {
      "id": "big-three",
      "name": "The Big Three (context, model, prompt)",
      "plain_english": "The three primitives of phase-1 AI coding: what the model can see (context), which model does the work (model), and what you ask for (prompt). Every AI coding interaction is governed by these whether you notice or not.",
      "dan_words": "\"With AI coding, you've been interacting with the big three: context, model, prompt. This is a principle of AI coding. It's always there even if you can't see it.\"",
      "misconception": "That the big three become obsolete in phase 2. They remain the foundation; phase 2 adds exactly one new dimension on top."
    },
    {

# Agent Experts: Finally, Agents That Actually Learn
**Lesson #13 (Advanced)**  ·  https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/agent-experts

_The massive problem with agents is they forget - and that means they don't learn. Agent Experts solve this with a three-step workflow: Act, Learn, Reuse._

## Loot Box — 12 notes

### 🔥 The Massive Problem: Agents Forget
Traditional software improves as it's used, storing analytics and patterns. Agents of today don't - they forget everything between sessions. This is the problem Agent Experts solve.

### 🏆 The Act-Learn-Reuse Pattern
Transform forgetful agents into learning machines: Act (take useful actions), Learn (store new information), Reuse (apply expertise on next execution). No human in the loop required.

### 🔥 Mental Models: The Data Structure of Expertise
A mental model is a data structure that evolves over time. With each useful action, experts accumulate information, examples, and expertise around specific topics. This is how real experts work.

### 🔥 Self-Improving Template Meta Prompts
An Agent Expert is a concrete form of a self-improving template meta prompt. Prompts that build other prompts, with specific structure, that update themselves with new information for the next execution.

### 🔥 Meta Agentics: Build The System That Builds
Meta prompts, meta agents, meta skills - these help you build your agentic layer faster. Every codebase must have meta agentics. Prompts writing prompts, agents building agents, skills building skills.

### ⚔️ TAC Lesson 13 - Agent Experts Repository
git clone https://github.com/disler/agent-experts.git

### 🔥 Expertise Files: External Mental Models
Expertise files are isolated markdown files that store your agent's accumulated knowledge. Unlike memory files, they're topic-specific and updated by the self-improve prompt, not manually.

### 💎 Never Update Expertise Files Directly
The key insight: don't update expertise files manually. Teach your agents HOW to learn by updating the self-improve prompt. Let agents maintain their own expertise over time.

### 🔥 Codebase Experts for High-Risk Systems
Deploy codebase experts for critical areas: billing systems, security modules, database operations. These agents accumulate domain knowledge and reduce errors in high-complexity, high-risk code.

### 🔥 Product-Focused Agent Experts
Beyond code, agent experts can power adaptive user experiences. Product experts learn user patterns and preferences, creating intelligent systems that improve with usage.

### 🏆 Tactic: Build Agents That Learn
The full tactic: Create self-improving template meta prompts with expertise files. Let agents Act, Learn, and Reuse knowledge autonomously. Transform forgetful agents into domain experts.

### 🏆 When to Build Agent Experts
Build experts when: high complexity requires accumulated knowledge, error rates need reduction over time, domain-specific patterns emerge. Generic agents suffice for simple, stateless tasks. argument-hint: [check_git_diff (true/false)] [focus_area (optional)]
---

# Purpose

You maintain the WebSocket expert system's expertise accuracy by comparing the existing expertise file against the actual codebase implementation. It follows the `Workflow` section to detect and remedy any differences, missing pieces, or outdated information, ensuring the expertise file remains a powerful **mental model** and accurate memory reference for WebSocket-related tasks.

## Variables

CHECK_GIT_DIFF: $1 default to false if not specified
FOCUS_AREA: $2 default to empty string
EXPERTISE_FILE: .claude/commands/experts/websocket/expertise.yaml
MAX_LINES: 1000

## Instructions

- This is a self-improvement workflow to keep WebSocket expertise synchronized with the actual codebase
- Think of the expertise file as your **mental model** and memory reference for all WebSocket-related functionality
- Always validate expertise against real implementation, not assumptions
- Focus exclusively on WebSocket-related functionality throughout the codebase
- If FOCUS_AREA is provided, prioritize validation and updates for that specific area
- Maintain the YAML structure of the expertise file
- Enforce strict line limit of 1000 lines maximum
- Prioritize actionable, high-value expertise over verbose documentation
- When trimming, remove least critical information that won't impact expert performance
- Git diff checking is optional and controlled by the CHECK_GIT_DIFF variable
- Be thorough in validation but concise in documentation
- Don't include 'summaries' of work done in your expertise when a git diff is checked. Focus on true, important information that pertains to the key websocket functionality and implementation.
- Write as a principle engineer that writes CLEARLY and CONCISELY for future engineers so they can easily understand how to read and update functionality surrounding the websocket implementation.
- Keep in mind, after your thorough search, there may be nothing to be done - this is perfectly acceptable. If there's nothing to be done, report that and stop.

## Workflow

1. **Check Git Diff (Conditional)**
   - If CHECK_GIT_DIFF is "true", run `git diff` to identify recent changes to WebSocket-related files
   - If changes detected, note them for targeted validation in step 3
   - If CHECK_GIT_DIFF is "false", skip this step

2. **Read Current Expertise**
   - Read the entire EXPERTISE_FILE to understand current documented expertise
   - Identify key sections: overview, core_implementation, event_types, streaming_architecture, etc.
   - Note any areas that seem outdated or incomplete

3. **Validate Against Codebase**
   - Read the EXPERTISE_FILE to identify which files are documented as key implementation files
   - Read those files to understand current implementation
   - Use Grep to search for WebSocket event types, broadcast methods, and connection handling
   - Compare documented expertise against actual code:
     - Event types and their fields
     - Broadcast methods and their signatures
     - File locations and line numbers
     - Architecture patterns and data flows
     - Hook integration points
     - Frontend integration patterns
   - If FOCUS_AREA is provided, prioritize validation of that specific area
   - If git diff was checked in step 1, pay special attention to changed areas

4. **Identify Discrepancies**
   - List all differences found:
     - Missing events or methods in expertise file
     - Outdated line numbers or file paths
     - Changed method signatures or parameters
     - New features not documented
     - Removed features still documented
     - Incorrect architecture descriptions

5. **Update Expertise File**
   - Remedy all identified discrepancies by updating EXPERTISE_FILE
   - Add missing information
   - Update outdated information
   - Remove obsolete information
   - Maintain YAML structure and formatting
   - Ensure all file paths and line numbers are accurate
   - Keep descriptions concise and actionable

       - Overly verbose descriptions
       - Redundant examples
       - Low-priority edge cases
       - Excessive detail in less critical areas
     - Trim identified sections
     - Run line count check again
     - REPEAT this sub-workflow until line count ≤ MAX_LINES
   - Document what was trimmed in the report

7. **Validation Check**
   - Read the updated EXPERTISE_FILE
   - Verify all critical WebSocket information is present
   - Ensure line count is within limit
   - Validate YAML syntax by compiling the file:
     - Run: `python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('EXPERTISE_FILE'))"`
     - Replace EXPERTISE_FILE with the actual path from the variable
     - Confirm no syntax errors are raised
     - If errors occur, fix the YAML structure and re-validate

### Summary
- Brief overview of self-improvement execution

  - Confirmation that trimming didn't impact critical expertise

- Confirm all critical WebSocket expertise is present
- Confirm line count is within limit
- Note any areas that may need future attention

### Codebase References
- List of files validated against with line numbers where relevant
- Key methods and functions verified

Summary:

- Discrepancies remedied: 8

Codebase References:

1	---
2	name: Start Orchestrator
3	description: Starts the Orchestrator 3 Stream application (backend + frontend) in background mode. Use when the user asks to start orchestrator, launch orchestrator, run orchestrator, or open the orchestrator UI. Supports --session and --cwd flags for backend.
4	---
5	
6	# Start Orchestrator
7	
8	Launches the Orchestrator 3 Stream application with both backend (FastAPI) and frontend (Vue/Vite) servers.
9	
10	## Prerequisites
11	
12	- The orchestrator application is located at `apps/orchestrator_3_stream/`
13	- Backend requires Python with uv (Astral UV)
14	- Frontend requires Node.js with npm
15	- PostgreSQL database should be running
16	
17	## Configuration
18	
19	Default ports (configurable via `.env`):
20	- **Backend**: Port 8002 (default fallback: 9403)
21	- **Frontend**: Port 5175
22	
23	## Backend Flags
24	
25	The backend script (`start_be.sh`) accepts:
26	
27	| Flag | Description | Priority |
28	|------|-------------|----------|
29	| `--cwd <path>` | Working directory for the orchestrator | CLI > .env (`ORCHESTRATOR_WORKING_DIR`) > current dir |
30	| `--session <id>` | Session ID to resume | CLI > .env (`ORCHESTRATOR_SESSION_ID`) > new session |
31	
32	## Workflow
33	
34	### 1. Start Backend (with optional flags)
35	
36	Run in background by default:
37	
38	```bash
39	# Basic start (new session, current directory)
40	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh &
41	
42	# With session ID (resume existing session)
43	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --session <session-id> &
44	
45	# With custom working directory
46	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --cwd /path/to/project &
47	
48	# With both flags
49	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --cwd /path/to/project --session <session-id> &
50	```
51	
52	### 2. Start Frontend
53	
54	Run in background:
55	
56	```bash
57	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
58	```
59	
60	### 3. Open UI in Chrome
61	
62	After both services are running, open the frontend URL:
63	
64	```bash
65	open -a "Google Chrome" "http://127.0.0.1:5175"
66	```
67	
68	## Complete Example Commands
69	
70	**Start both in background (new session):**
71	```bash
72	# Start backend
73	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh &
74	
75	# Wait for backend to initialize
76	sleep 3
77	
78	# Start frontend
79	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
80	
81	# Wait for frontend to initialize
82	sleep 2
83	
84	# Open in Chrome
85	open -a "Google Chrome" "http://127.0.0.1:5175"
86	```
87	
88	**Resume a session:**
89	```bash
90	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --session abc123-def456 &
91	sleep 3
92	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
93	sleep 2
94	open -a "Google Chrome" "http://127.0.0.1:5175"
95	```
96	
97	## Foreground Mode
98	
99	If user requests foreground mode, do NOT use `&` suffix and run each command sequentially, starting frontend first in background then backend in foreground:
100	
101	```bash
102	# Frontend in background (so we can run backend in foreground)
103	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
104	
105	# Backend in foreground (to see logs)
106	cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --cwd /path/to/project
107	```
108	
109	## Stopping Services
110	
111	To stop the services:
112	
113	```bash
114	# Find and kill backend
115	lsof -ti:8002 | xargs kill -9
116	
117	# Find and kill frontend
118	lsof -ti:5175 | xargs kill -9
119	```
120	
121	## Troubleshooting
122	
123	- **Port in use**: The scripts automatically kill processes using their ports before starting
124	- **Database not running**: Ensure PostgreSQL is running before starting backend
125	- **Missing dependencies**: Run `uv sync` in backend directory, `npm install` in frontend directory
126	
127	## Examples
128	
129	### Example 1: Basic Start
130	
131	User request:
132	```
133	Start the orchestrator
134	```
135	
136	You would:
137	1. Start backend in background:
138	   ```bash
139	   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh &
140	   ```
141	2. Wait 3 seconds for backend to initialize
142	3. Start frontend in background:
143	   ```bash
144	   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
145	   ```
146	4. Wait 2 seconds for frontend to initialize
147	5. Open Chrome:
148	   ```bash
149	   open -a "Google Chrome" "http://127.0.0.1:5175"
150	   ```
151	
152	### Example 2: Resume Session with Custom CWD
153	
154	User request:
155	```
156	Start orchestrator with session abc123 and working directory /Users/me/myproject
157	```
158	
159	You would:
160	1. Start backend with flags:
161	   ```bash
162	   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --cwd /Users/me/myproject --session abc123 &
163	   ```
164	2. Wait, then start frontend and open Chrome as above
165	
166	### Example 3: Foreground Mode
167	
168	User request:
169	```
170	Start orchestrator in foreground so I can see logs
171	```
172	
173	You would:
174	1. Start frontend in background first:
175	   ```bash
176	   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
177	   ```
178	2. Wait 2 seconds
179	3. Start backend in foreground (no `&`):
180	   ```bash
181	   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh
182	   ```
183	4. Note: Chrome opening should happen after frontend is ready but before backend foreground command
184

description: Starts the Orchestrator 3 Stream application (backend + frontend) in background mode. Use when the user asks to start orchestrator, launch orchestrator, run orchestrator, or open the orchestrator UI. Supports --session and --cwd flags for backend.
---

# Start Orchestrator

Launches the Orchestrator 3 Stream application with both backend (FastAPI) and frontend (Vue/Vite) servers.

## Prerequisites

- The orchestrator application is located at `apps/orchestrator_3_stream/`
- Backend requires Python with uv (Astral UV)
- Frontend requires Node.js with npm
- PostgreSQL database should be running

## Configuration

Default ports (configurable via `.env`):
- **Backend**: Port 8002 (default fallback: 9403)
- **Frontend**: Port 5175

## Backend Flags

The backend script (`start_be.sh`) accepts:

| Flag | Description | Priority |
|------|-------------|----------|
| `--cwd <path>` | Working directory for the orchestrator | CLI > .env (`ORCHESTRATOR_WORKING_DIR`) > current dir |
| `--session <id>` | Session ID to resume | CLI > .env (`ORCHESTRATOR_SESSION_ID`) > new session |

## Workflow

### 1. Start Backend (with optional flags)

Run in background by default:

```bash
# Basic start (new session, current directory)
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh &

# With session ID (resume existing session)
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --session <session-id> &

# With custom working directory
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --cwd /path/to/project &

# With both flags
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --cwd /path/to/project --session <session-id> &
```

### 2. Start Frontend

Run in background:

```bash
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
```

### 3. Open UI in Chrome

After both services are running, open the frontend URL:

```bash
open -a "Google Chrome" "http://127.0.0.1:5175"
```

## Complete Example Commands

**Start both in background (new session):**
```bash
# Start backend
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh &

# Wait for backend to initialize
sleep 3

# Start frontend
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &

# Wait for frontend to initialize
sleep 2

# Open in Chrome
open -a "Google Chrome" "http://127.0.0.1:5175"
```

**Resume a session:**
```bash
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --session abc123-def456 &
sleep 3
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
sleep 2
open -a "Google Chrome" "http://127.0.0.1:5175"
```

## Foreground Mode

If user requests foreground mode, do NOT use `&` suffix and run each command sequentially, starting frontend first in background then backend in foreground:

```bash
# Frontend in background (so we can run backend in foreground)
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &

# Backend in foreground (to see logs)
cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --cwd /path/to/project
```

## Stopping Services

To stop the services:

```bash
# Find and kill backend
lsof -ti:8002 | xargs kill -9

# Find and kill frontend
lsof -ti:5175 | xargs kill -9
```

## Troubleshooting

- **Port in use**: The scripts automatically kill processes using their ports before starting
- **Database not running**: Ensure PostgreSQL is running before starting backend
- **Missing dependencies**: Run `uv sync` in backend directory, `npm install` in frontend directory

## Examples

### Example 1: Basic Start

User request:
```
Start the orchestrator
```

You would:
1. Start backend in background:
   ```bash
   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh &
   ```
2. Wait 3 seconds for backend to initialize
3. Start frontend in background:
   ```bash
   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
   ```
4. Wait 2 seconds for frontend to initialize
5. Open Chrome:
   ```bash
   open -a "Google Chrome" "http://127.0.0.1:5175"
   ```

### Example 2: Resume Session with Custom CWD

User request:
```
Start orchestrator with session abc123 and working directory /Users/me/myproject
```

You would:
1. Start backend with flags:
   ```bash
   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh --cwd /Users/me/myproject --session abc123 &
   ```
2. Wait, then start frontend and open Chrome as above

### Example 3: Foreground Mode

User request:
```
Start orchestrator in foreground so I can see logs
```

You would:
1. Start frontend in background first:
   ```bash
   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_fe.sh &
   ```
2. Wait 2 seconds
3. Start backend in foreground (no `&`):
   ```bash
   cd /path/to/agent-experts/apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh
   ```
4. Note: Chrome opening should happen after frontend is ready but before backend foreground command

# Purpose

Create new Agent Skills for AI Agents by following a structured workflow based on best practices and comprehensive documentation.

## Instructions

This skill helps you create new Agent Skills for Claude Code. Before starting, read the comprehensive documentation files in the [docs/](docs/) directory for complete context.

### Prerequisites

**Required Reading** - Read these files in order before creating a skill:
1. [docs/claude_code_agent_skills.md](docs/claude_code_agent_skills.md) - Complete guide to creating and managing skills
2. [docs/claude_code_agent_skills_overview.md](docs/claude_code_agent_skills_overview.md) - Architecture and how skills work
3. [docs/blog_equipping_agents_with_skills.md](docs/blog_equipping_agents_with_skills.md) - Design principles and best practices

### Understanding Skills

**What is a Skill?**
- A directory containing a `SKILL.md` file with YAML frontmatter
- Instructions that Claude loads on-demand when relevant
- Optional supporting files (scripts, documentation, templates)
- Like an onboarding guide for a new team member

**Three Sources of Skills:**
1. **Personal Skills**: `~/.claude/skills/` - Available across all your projects
2. **Project Skills**: `.claude/skills/` - Shared with team via git
3. **Plugin Skills**: Bundled with Claude Code plugins, automatically available when installed

**Progressive Disclosure (3 Levels):**
1. **Metadata** (always loaded): `name` and `description` in YAML frontmatter
2. **Instructions** (loaded when triggered): Main body of SKILL.md
3. **Resources** (loaded as needed): Additional files, scripts, templates

**Key Principle:** Only relevant content enters the context window at any time.

### Skill Creation Workflow

#### Step 1: Define the Skill's Purpose

Ask the user these questions:
1. What task or domain should this skill cover?
2. When should Claude use this skill? (triggers)
3. What expertise or workflows need to be captured?
4. Does it need scripts, templates, or other resources?

Document the answers for reference.

#### Step 2: Create the Skill Directory Structure

Create skills in the project's `.claude/skills/` directory for team sharing:

```bash
mkdir -p .claude/skills/<skill-name>
```

**Naming conventions:**
- **Use gerund form** (verb + -ing): `processing-pdfs`, `analyzing-spreadsheets`, `managing-databases`
- Must contain only **lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens**
- Maximum 64 characters
- Cannot contain XML tags or reserved words ("anthropic", "claude")
- Avoid generic names like `helper`, `utils`, `tools`

**Note:** Project skills (`.claude/skills/`) are automatically shared with your team via git. For personal skills only you use, create in `~/.claude/skills/` instead.

#### Step 3: Design the SKILL.md Structure

Every skill must have:
```yaml
---
name: Your Skill Name
description: Brief description of what this Skill does and when to use it
---

# Your Skill Name

## Instructions
[Clear, step-by-step guidance for Claude]

## Examples
[Concrete examples of using this Skill]
```

**Frontmatter Requirements:**
- `name`: Required
  - Max 64 characters
  - **Lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only**
  - Cannot contain XML tags or reserved words ("anthropic", "claude")
  - Use gerund form: `processing-pdfs`, `analyzing-data`
- `description`: Required, max 1024 characters
  - **MUST be written in third person** (critical for discovery)
  - Include BOTH what it does AND when to use it
  - Mention key trigger words/phrases
  - Be specific, not vague
  - Cannot contain XML tags

**Optional Frontmatter (Claude Code only):**
- `allowed-tools`: Restrict which tools Claude can use (e.g., `Read, Grep, Glob`)

#### Step 4: Write the Instructions Section

**Structure the instructions as:**
1. **Prerequisites** - Required dependencies, tools, environment setup
2. **Workflow** - Step-by-step process (numbered steps)
3. **Supporting Details** - Additional context, script usage, error handling

**Best Practices:**
- Use clear, actionable language
- Number sequential steps
- Use bullet points for options/lists
- Include code blocks with bash commands
- Reference supporting files with relative links: `[reference.md](reference.md)`
- Keep focused on one capability
- **Keep SKILL.md body under 500 lines** for optimal performance
- **Avoid deeply nested references** - keep references one level deep from SKILL.md
- For files over 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top

**Example workflow format:**
```markdown
### Workflow

1. **First step description**:
   ```bash
   command to run
   ```
   - Additional context

# Purpose

You are an adaptive shopping expert for Nile. Generate personalized home page sections by analyzing user behavior data and **streaming each section immediately** using the `stream_section` tool. Each section appears on the user's screen as soon as you call the tool.

## Variables

### Dynamic Variables (Injected at Runtime)

#### TOTAL_IMPROVEMENTS:

```json
{{TOTAL_IMPROVEMENTS}}
```

#### CHECKED_OUT_PRODUCTS (Full Product Objects - Highest Signal):

```json
{{CHECKED_OUT_PRODUCTS}}
```

#### ADDED_TO_CART_PRODUCTS (Full Product Objects - Medium Signal):

```json
{{ADDED_TO_CART_PRODUCTS}}
```

#### VIEWED_PRODUCTS (Full Product Objects - Low Signal):

```json
{{VIEWED_PRODUCTS}}
```

#### AVAILABLE_CATEGORIES (All product categories):

```json
{{AVAILABLE_CATEGORIES}}
```

#### AVAILABLE_BRANDS (All product brands):

```json
{{AVAILABLE_BRANDS}}
```

### Static Variables (Configuration)

SECTIONS_RANGE: 4-6
PRODUCTS_PER_SECTION_RANGE: 6-12
TOTAL_PRODUCTS: SECTIONS_RANGE × PRODUCTS_PER_SECTION_RANGE

## Instructions

### User Expertise Priority

Prioritize user signals in this order (strongest to weakest):

1. **CHECKED_OUT_PRODUCTS** - Strongest signal (they purchased it!)
2. **ADDED_TO_CART_PRODUCTS** - Medium signal (showed purchase intent)
3. **VIEWED_PRODUCTS** - Weak signal (browsed it)

Also prioritize recency as a secondary signal and sometimes a primary signal if the checked out products are not relevant to the new items added to the cart or viewed. That means we have a new set of products that the user is interested in.

### New User Defaults (No Expertise)

If TOTAL_IMPROVEMENTS is 0 or all product lists are empty:

- Use `generic-slogan` for the greeting (not `specific-slogan`)
- Call `find_related_products` to discover products (try different categories, top-rated items)
- Build an engaging discovery experience to help them explore

### Component Selection Rules

- With the exception of the 'specific-slogan' component, be sure to include several list based components to keep the user engaged.
- We'll also want to veer off the related products and just show some new products that the user may not have seen before to kick off new interests.

| Component         | When to Use                                       |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `specific-slogan` | Opening message for personalized users            |
| `specific-upsell` | Upsell based on purchases (use product from data) |
| `carousel`        | Horizontal scroll for related products            |
| `card`            | Standard product display                          |
| `super-card`      | Premium display                                   |
| `basic-square`    | Grid layout for varied products                   |

### Product ID Patterns

Components use either multiple products or a single product:

- **Multiple products** (`product_ids`): carousel, card, basic-square
- **Single product** (`product_id`): super-card, specific-upsell

### Critical Rules - STREAMING MODE

- **STREAM EACH SECTION IMMEDIATELY** using `stream_section` tool
- Call `stream_section` once for EACH section - user sees it instantly
- Do NOT output JSON - use the tool instead
- Extract product IDs from the data above
- The system hydrates full product data automatically
- **EXCLUDE CART ITEMS** - Never include products from ADDED_TO_CART_PRODUCTS in your sections (user already has them)
- ALWAYS add AT LEAST 3 products to each section when dealing with a multiple product section.

## Workflow

### Step 1: Stream Personalized Greeting FIRST

Immediately call `stream_section` with a `specific-slogan`:

```
stream_section({
  component_type: "specific-slogan",
  slogan_text: "Welcome back!",
  subtitle: "Based on your interest in [category]"
})
```

### Step 2: Build and Stream Sections

IMPORTANT: In a loop until you have TOTAL_PRODUCTS products across SECTIONS_RANGE sections:

1. Call `find_related_products` if you need more products
2. Call `stream_section` to display a section

Mix user data with discovered products for variety. 
Mix in some new products that the user may not have seen before to kick off new interests.
Before you move on to the next section, make sure you have these 2 things:

- You have TOTAL_PRODUCTS products across SECTIONS_RANGE sections
- You have a new set of products that the user may not have seen before to kick off new interests.

### Step 3: Complete

After streaming SECTIONS_RANGE sections and a total of TOTAL_PRODUCTS products, you're done. No final output needed.

## Tool Reference

### stream_section

Stream a section to the user immediately.

| Parameter      | Type      | Description                                      |
| -------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| component_type | string    | carousel, card, specific-slogan, super-card, etc |
| title          | string    | Section title (for product sections)             |
| subtitle       | string    | Subtitle (for slogans/upsells)                   |
| slogan_text    | string    | Main text (for specific-slogan)                  |
| product_ids    | list[int] | Product IDs for carousel/card/basic-square       |
| product_id     | int       | Single product ID for super-card/specific-upsell |

### find_related_products

Search for products by category, brand, price range, or rating.

| Parameter  | Type   | Description                    |
| ---------- | ------ | ------------------------------ |
| category   | string | Product category               |
| brand      | string | Brand name                     |
| min_price  | number | Minimum price filter           |
| max_price  | number | Maximum price filter           |
| min_rating | number | Minimum rating filter (1-5)    |
| limit      | int    | Max products to return (def 8) |

## Example Flow

1. `stream_section` → specific-slogan (user sees greeting!)
2. `stream_section` → card with viewed product IDs (user sees products!)
3. `find_related_products` → get related products
4. `stream_section` → carousel with related IDs (user sees more!)
5. `stream_section` → basic-square with more IDs (user sees grid!)
6. Done - all sections streamed!

"""Expertise model for Agent Expert learning."""
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, Integer, JSON
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship
from ..database import Base


class Expertise(Base):
    """User expertise model - the Agent Expert's 'mental model'."""
    __tablename__ = "expertise"

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"), unique=True, index=True)
    total_improvements: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(Integer, default=0)
    last_improvement_at: Mapped[Optional[datetime]] = mapped_column(nullable=True)
    expertise_data: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(JSON, default=dict)

    # Relationships
    user = relationship("User", back_populates="expertise")

    def get_default_expertise(self) -> dict:
        """Return default expertise structure."""
        return {
            "viewed_products": [],
            "added_to_cart": [],
            "checked_out": []
        }

from ..config import ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

from ..schemas import (
    HomePageResponse,

    HydratedProduct,

    AgentSectionRaw,

# Configure logger
logger = logging.getLogger("nile.agent_expert")
logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

# Add console handler if not already present
if not logger.handlers:
    handler = logging.StreamHandler()
    handler.setFormatter(
        logging.Formatter(
            "%(asctime)s | %(levelname)-8s | %(name)s | %(message)s", datefmt="%H:%M:%S"
        )
    )
    logger.addHandler(handler)

# Module-level storage for tool execution context
_current_db: Optional[AsyncSession] = None
_current_user_id: Optional[int] = None

# Prompt file paths

_USER_PROMPT_PATH = _PROMPTS_DIR / "shopping_expert_user_prompt.md"


@tool(
    "find_related_products",
    "Search for products by category, brand, price range, or rating. All parameters are optional - only provide the filters you need.",

        "category": str,
        "brand": str,
        "min_price": float,
        "max_price": float,
        "min_rating": float,
        "limit": int,
    },
)
async def find_related_products_tool(args: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:

        min_price: Minimum price filter
        max_price: Maximum price filter
        min_rating: Minimum rating filter (1-5)

    category = args.get("category") if args.get("category") else None

    min_price = float(args["min_price"]) if args.get("min_price") else None
    max_price = float(args["max_price"]) if args.get("max_price") else None

# WebSocket Implementation Expertise
# Multi-Agent Orchestration System - Real-Time Communication Architecture

overview:
  description: "FastAPI WebSocket-based event bus for real-time communication between backend services and frontend clients"
  primary_endpoint: "/ws"
  default_url: "ws://127.0.0.1:9403/ws"
  architecture_pattern: "Centralized WebSocketManager with one-to-many broadcast"
  integration_depth: "Deep integration with Claude SDK hooks for real-time agent execution events"

core_implementation:
  websocket_manager:
    file: "apps/orchestrator_3_stream/backend/modules/websocket_manager.py"
    lines: 260
    purpose: "Centralized connection manager and event broadcaster"

    state_management:
      active_connections:
        type: "List[WebSocket]"
        description: "All active WebSocket connections"
      connection_metadata:
        type: "Dict[WebSocket, dict]"
        description: "Metadata per connection (client_id, connected_at)"

    lifecycle_methods:
      connect:
        lines: "25-53"
        flow:
          - "Accept WebSocket handshake"
          - "Add to active_connections list"
          - "Create metadata with client_id and connected_at timestamp"
          - "Send connection_established message with client ID"

      disconnect:
        lines: "55-69"
        flow:
          - "Remove from active_connections list"
          - "Delete metadata entry"
          - "Log disconnection with connection count"
        triggered_by:
          - "WebSocketDisconnect exception"
          - "Failed send operation"
          - "Explicit disconnect call"

      send_to_client:
        lines: "71-80"
        behavior: "Send JSON to single client, auto-disconnect on failure"
        error_handling: "Catches all exceptions, calls disconnect on failure"

      broadcast:
        lines: "82-111"
        behavior: "Send JSON to all connected clients (with optional exclude)"
        error_handling: "Tracks disconnected clients, cleans up after broadcast"
        concurrency: "Safe for concurrent calls"

  fastapi_endpoint:
    file: "apps/orchestrator_3_stream/backend/main.py"
    lines: "664-698"
    route: "@app.websocket('/ws')"

    handler_flow:
      - "await ws_manager.connect(websocket)"
      - "Enter infinite receive loop"
      - "Parse incoming JSON by 'type' field"
      - "Handle keep-alive pings"
      - "Catch WebSocketDisconnect and cleanup"

    incoming_message_types:
      - "ping"
      - "heartbeat"
      - "client_message (future use)"

# also merged ~every 12s blocks
blocks=[]
buf=[]

if buf: blocks.append((bt or 0,' '.join(buf)))
with open('/tmp/ah5_blocks.txt','w') as o:

PY

1	# TAC-1 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)
2	
3	TAC-1 ages unusually well because it teaches primitives, and Dan future-proofs on camera: *"Your Claude Code UI might look different. You might be using newer models. That's all great... Don't let that distract you from the value embedded in each lesson."* Still, five things have moved. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Reusable agent behavior: prompt files → Agent Skills  ⟵ the big named gap
8	
9	**Course era:** reusable behavior is encoded as a raw prompt file (`programmable/prompt.md`) plus launcher scripts. Works, but discovery, triggering, and composition are all manual.
10	**Current:** Agent Skills are the first-class encoding — `SKILL.md` files with frontmatter (name, description, trigger guidance), loaded on demand by Claude Code and shareable across projects/teams. Skills are the modern answer to "how do I package the thing my agent knows how to do?" — exactly the question `programmable/` answers primitively.
11	**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED. This is the course's most-cited gap ("Skills as modern encoding of engineering"). Teach prompt.md first (pedagogically perfect: no magic), then show the same workflow as a Skill.
12	**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
13	
14	## 2. Embedding: bare `claude -p` → headless mode + Claude Agent SDK
15	
16	**Course era:** `claude -p "<prompt>"` via subprocess from sh/ts/py; output captured as plain text; REPORT requested inside the prompt itself.
17	**Current:** the pattern survives verbatim (and remains the best teaching form), but production embedding now uses headless flags — `--output-format json|stream-json`, `--allowedTools`, `--permission-mode`, session resume — and, for real systems, the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS): structured outputs, hooks, subagents, multi-turn control. What TAC-1 calls "programmable agentic coding" grew into a supported product surface.
18	**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the 3-line script you just wrote has a grown-up form"), not a rewrite — concept unchanged: agent as callable component.
19	**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
20	
21	## 3. Permissions: flat allowlist → modes, hooks, sandboxing
22	
23	**Course era:** `.claude/settings.json` with a flat `permissions.allow` list (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash(uv run:*)`, four git patterns, `WebSearch`).
24	**Current:** that syntax still works, but the surface grew: permission modes (plan/accept-edits/etc.), pre/post tool-use hooks, sandboxed bash, deny rules, and settings layering (user/project/local). Teams gate agents with hooks, not just allowlists.
25	**Book treatment:** footnote + "current practice" callout. The lesson's HABIT — always read what the agent may do before running it — transfers unchanged and is the actual teaching point.
26	**Overlay:** none needed.
27	
28	## 4. Models & UI: period detail, pre-handled by Dan
29	
30	**Course era:** course-era Claude models and TUI; Aider cited as the phase-1 analogue.
31	**Current:** newer model families (Claude 4.x → Claude 5 era), richer TUI, plan modes, background tasks. None of it invalidates a frame of the lesson — the demo is deliberately primitive-level.
32	**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected screenshots ("UI is period detail; the flow is identical today"). No overlay.
33	
34	## 5. Scale: one serial loop → fleets, subagents, parallel worktrees
35	
36	**Course era:** one agent, one workflow, serially, in one terminal — deliberately, since it's lesson 1 of 8.
37	**Current:** the same agentic prompt is routinely fanned out: subagents, background tasks, git-worktree-isolated parallel runs, orchestrated pipelines. "Systems that build systems" now has industrial-strength machinery.
38	**Book treatment:** forward-pointer only ("the course scales this in later lessons; today's ceiling is higher still"). Overlaying scale content on lesson 1 would front-run the pedagogy.
39	**Overlay candidates (deferred to later chapters):** `fop_yxV-mPo` — *Codebase Singularity*; `hGg3nWp7afg` — *3 Codebase Folders* (both include_in_phase1: **no**).
40	
41	---
42	
43	## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)
44	
45	- The phase-1/phase-2 frame and "AI coding is not enough" — if anything, more consensus now than at recording.
46	- The core four. Context/model/prompt/tools remains the complete diagnostic vocabulary for agentic failures.
47	- The agentic prompt as workflow-specification (RUN/CREATE/RUN/REPORT) — this shape is now everywhere (slash commands, skills, CI prompts).
48	- "Scale and performance, not novelty" as the right lens on tool calling.
49	- The three-essential-elements checklist for evaluating agentic tools.
50	- Terminal ubiquity as the embedding superpower.
51	- Report-back as the first closed-loop habit.
52	- The economics: token spend as pay-to-play. (Costs shifted; the logic didn't.)
53	
54	## Phase-1 overlay decision (strict, per brief: max 1–3)
55	
56	| # | Video | Maps to | Include |
57	|---|---|---|---|
58	| 1 | `2TIXl2rlA6Q` — AI Coding is NOT ENOUGH | operationalizes tactic (lesson thesis, phase model) | ✅ |
59	| 2 | `6fCqj4xFCZI` — How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever | named hole (form factor + programmable embedding, current state) | ✅ |
60	| 3 | `X2ciJedw2vU` — RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL | corrects outdated (skills gap) | ✅ |
61	| 4 | `fop_yxV-mPo` — Codebase Singularity | self-operating vision → later lessons | ❌ defer |
62	| 5 | `hGg3nWp7afg` — 3 Codebase Folders | context engineering → later lessons | ❌ defer |
63	
64	*Caveat: IDs/titles from the orchestration brief's seed list; verify each resolves and content matches title before publishing overlay links (no video fetching was performed in this extract pass, per brief).*

1	# TAC-1 Lab Spec — Hello Agentic Coding
2	
3	**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → `tac/tac-1`; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git`). No external repos, no extra dependencies beyond the lesson's prerequisite tools.
4	**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you type **zero** lines of application code by hand. Even file edits in the stretch drills go through Claude Code.
5	**Time box:** 45–75 minutes. Token cost: one interactive demo pair + 3–5 headless runs (small; but real — pay to play).
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 0 · Setup (10 min)
10	
11	1. Fresh directory for TAC codebases → `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git && cd tac-1`
12	2. Verify the toolbelt: `claude --version`, `uv --version`, `git --version`; optional `bun --version` (TS variant). Windows: run everything inside WSL.
13	3. **Permissions audit (do not skip):** open `.claude/settings.json` and answer in writing:
14	   - Which three file tools may the agent use freely?
15	   - Which four git subcommands are allowed? Which git subcommands are NOT (e.g. `push`)?
16	   - What single non-local tool is enabled? (`WebSearch`)
17	4. Open the repo in your IDE, open the terminal (Cmd+J in VS Code), run `claude`.
18	
19	**Checkpoint 0:** you can state, without looking, what the agent may do. If you can't, re-read the file — this habit is a graded outcome.
20	
21	## 1 · Reproduce Dan — interactive A/B (15 min)
22	
23	**A. Phase-1 prompt.** Copy the README **AI Coding Prompt** into Claude Code; fire.
24	- Verify: `main_aic.py` exists; `uv run main_aic.py` → `goodbye ai coding`.
25	- Note what did NOT happen: no branch, no commit, no execution by the agent.
26	
27	**B. Phase-2 prompt.** Copy the README **Agentic Coding Prompt**; fire. Watch the todo checklist form, then drain.
28	- Verify all five engineering actions:
29	  1. `git branch --show-current` → `demo-agentic-coding`
30	  2. `main_tac.py` exists; `uv run main_tac.py` → `hello agentic coding` + one-line AI-agent definition
31	  3. both files were executed by the agent (outputs visible in its trace)
32	  4. `git log --oneline -1` → `Demo agentic coding capabilities`
33	  5. the agent reported what it did and cleaned up its todos
34	
35	**Checkpoint 1 (write it down):** list the five actions prompt B performed that prompt A didn't. This list IS the AI-coding → agentic-coding delta.
36	
37	## 2 · Reproduce Dan — programmable/headless (15 min)
38	
39	1. Read `programmable/prompt.md`. Spot the two differences from the README agentic prompt *before* running anything: (a) it also CREATEs `main_aic.py` — self-contained, no dependency on drill 1; (b) it ends with a `REPORT:` block demanding the exact output of both .py files.
40	2. Clean slate exactly like Dan: `git checkout main && git branch -D demo-agentic-coding`
41	3. From a fresh terminal on `main`: `uv run python programmable/programmable.py` — hands off. No interaction allowed.
42	4. When it returns, verify: branch re-created, both files re-created, commit present, and the printed REPORT contains the exact outputs (cross-check by running both files yourself).
43	5. Run the same workflow via the other two launchers (reset the branch between runs):
44	   - `sh programmable/programmable.sh`
45	   - `bun run programmable/programmable.ts`
46	
47	**Checkpoint 2:** all three launchers drove the identical workflow. Say in one sentence why the language didn't matter. *(Claude Code runs in the terminal; anything with terminal access can call `claude -p` — the agent is a function.)*
48	
49	## 3 · Stretch drills (15–30 min, still zero hand-typing)
50	
51	**S1 — Extend the REPORT (closed-loop thinking).** Using Claude Code (not your editor), edit `programmable/prompt.md` so REPORT also includes the current git branch name. Reset the branch; rerun the Python launcher; verify the report changed accordingly.
52	
53	**S2 — Fourth launcher (prove the pattern).** Ask Claude Code to add a launcher in another language available on your machine (e.g. plain Node, Ruby, Go — anything with terminal access), following the existing three as style guides. Reset; run it; verify the identical workflow.
54	
55	**S3 — Break the tool surface (permissions intuition).** Via Claude Code, remove `"Bash(git commit:*)"` from `.claude/settings.json`. Rerun the agentic prompt and observe precisely where and how the workflow halts or asks. Restore the permission. Write one sentence: what does this teach about the tools circle of the core four? *(The tool surface bounds what an agentic prompt can accomplish; permissions are part of the system design.)*

# TAC-1 Lab Spec — Hello Agentic Coding

**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → `tac/tac-1`; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git`). No external repos, no extra dependencies beyond the lesson's prerequisite tools.
**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you type **zero** lines of application code by hand. Even file edits in the stretch drills go through Claude Code.
**Time box:** 45–75 minutes. Token cost: one interactive demo pair + 3–5 headless runs (small; but real — pay to play).

---

## 0 · Setup (10 min)

1. Fresh directory for TAC codebases → `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git && cd tac-1`
2. Verify the toolbelt: `claude --version`, `uv --version`, `git --version`; optional `bun --version` (TS variant). Windows: run everything inside WSL.
3. **Permissions audit (do not skip):** open `.claude/settings.json` and answer in writing:
   - Which three file tools may the agent use freely?
   - Which four git subcommands are allowed? Which git subcommands are NOT (e.g. `push`)?
   - What single non-local tool is enabled? (`WebSearch`)
4. Open the repo in your IDE, open the terminal (Cmd+J in VS Code), run `claude`.

**Checkpoint 0:** you can state, without looking, what the agent may do. If you can't, re-read the file — this habit is a graded outcome.

## 1 · Reproduce Dan — interactive A/B (15 min)

**A. Phase-1 prompt.** Copy the README **AI Coding Prompt** into Claude Code; fire.
- Verify: `main_aic.py` exists; `uv run main_aic.py` → `goodbye ai coding`.
- Note what did NOT happen: no branch, no commit, no execution by the agent.

**B. Phase-2 prompt.** Copy the README **Agentic Coding Prompt**; fire. Watch the todo checklist form, then drain.
- Verify all five engineering actions:
  1. `git branch --show-current` → `demo-agentic-coding`
  2. `main_tac.py` exists; `uv run main_tac.py` → `hello agentic coding` + one-line AI-agent definition
  3. both files were executed by the agent (outputs visible in its trace)
  4. `git log --oneline -1` → `Demo agentic coding capabilities`
  5. the agent reported what it did and cleaned up its todos

**Checkpoint 1 (write it down):** list the five actions prompt B performed that prompt A didn't. This list IS the AI-coding → agentic-coding delta.

## 2 · Reproduce Dan — programmable/headless (15 min)

1. Read `programmable/prompt.md`. Spot the two differences from the README agentic prompt *before* running anything: (a) it also CREATEs `main_aic.py` — self-contained, no dependency on drill 1; (b) it ends with a `REPORT:` block demanding the exact output of both .py files.
2. Clean slate exactly like Dan: `git checkout main && git branch -D demo-agentic-coding`
3. From a fresh terminal on `main`: `uv run python programmable/programmable.py` — hands off. No interaction allowed.
4. When it returns, verify: branch re-created, both files re-created, commit present, and the printed REPORT contains the exact outputs (cross-check by running both files yourself).
5. Run the same workflow via the other two launchers (reset the branch between runs):
   - `sh programmable/programmable.sh`
   - `bun run programmable/programmable.ts`

**Checkpoint 2:** all three launchers drove the identical workflow. Say in one sentence why the language didn't matter. *(Claude Code runs in the terminal; anything with terminal access can call `claude -p` — the agent is a function.)*

## 3 · Stretch drills (15–30 min, still zero hand-typing)

**S1 — Extend the REPORT (closed-loop thinking).** Using Claude Code (not your editor), edit `programmable/prompt.md` so REPORT also includes the current git branch name. Reset the branch; rerun the Python launcher; verify the report changed accordingly.

**S2 — Fourth launcher (prove the pattern).** Ask Claude Code to add a launcher in another language available on your machine (e.g. plain Node, Ruby, Go — anything with terminal access), following the existing three as style guides. Reset; run it; verify the identical workflow.

**S3 — Break the tool surface (permissions intuition).** Via Claude Code, remove `"Bash(git commit:*)"` from `.claude/settings.json`. Rerun the agentic prompt and observe precisely where and how the workflow halts or asks. Restore the permission. Write one sentence: what does this teach about the tools circle of the core four? *(The tool surface bounds what an agentic prompt can accomplish; permissions are part of the system design.)*

**S4 — Map to your job (transfer).** Time drill 1A and 1B. Then write two lists from your actual work: tasks that are AI-coding-prompt-shaped vs agentic-coding-prompt-shaped. Circle the one agentic-shaped task you'd automate first with the `programmable/` pattern.

## Pass criteria (all required)

- [ ] Zero application code typed by hand anywhere in the lab
- [ ] Permissions audit answers correct (checkpoint 0)
- [ ] Five-action delta list correct (checkpoint 1)
- [ ] `demo-agentic-coding` branch exists with commit `Demo agentic coding capabilities` containing `main_aic.py` + `main_tac.py`
- [ ] `uv run main_tac.py` prints "hello agentic coding" + a one-line AI-agent definition
- [ ] All three (or four, with S2) launchers completed headlessly with a REPORT matching the real outputs
- [ ] Closing oral check, no notes: the core four; the one-dimension delta; Claude Code's three essential elements; the contradicting truth resolved in one sentence

## Instructor / self-check notes

- **Most common stall:** the "new/existing branch" wording — if the branch already exists from a prior run, the agent may reuse it and the student thinks something broke. Fix: always `git branch -D demo-agentic-coding` between runs (Dan does exactly this on camera at ~17:56).
- **Second stall:** running the programmable script from inside the `demo-agentic-coding` branch instead of `main` — teaches why runbooks state their starting state.
- **Cost anxiety:** each headless run is a small number of agent turns; the lab total is modest. If a student can't run it at all, the budget conversation (pay to play) is the actual lesson surfacing early.
- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** skills, triggers, parallelism, CI embedding — later lessons. Deflect scope creep to keep the primitive crisp.

    "why_uncomfortable": "Dan opens by calling this \"likely the most controversial lesson of Agentic Horizon\" and names three buckets of engineers: those who dismiss the idea, those who give it a shot, and those who say \"this is what I've been looking for.\" It's uncomfortable because it asks you to (1) accept that a file the AGENT writes and maintains itself — a YAML/markdown \"mental model\" — is a legitimate, valuable engineering artifact and NOT just \"another source of truth\" to distrust; (2) hand the maintenance of that knowledge entirely to the agent and never hand-edit it; (3) pay a real up-front cost — writing self-improve prompts to teach your agents how to learn — instead of re-prompting by hand forever; and (4) trust learning artifacts in exactly the highest-stakes systems (billing, security) where false expertise is scariest. The reframe that makes it coherent: you already run on a fuzzy, self-updating mental model; you're just giving your agents the same thing, in a file."
  },
  "mission": "Move up the stack one more time: stop building the application and build the system that builds the system — the agentic layer around your codebase. Give that layer agents that never stop learning, so the higher the complexity and risk of a system, the MORE valuable your agents become instead of less. The irreplaceable agentic engineer deploys experts that remember and improve, not generalists that boot up, forget, and force you to babysit memory files by hand. Agent experts are one of the killer building blocks of that layer — for your codebase (billing, security, database, integrations) and, as a seed of a whole new product class, for your users (per-user adaptive experiences).",
  "controversy_framing": {
    "dan_words": "There will be three buckets of engineers that watch this lesson. Those who dismiss this idea, those who give it a shot, and those who say, this is what I've been looking for.",
    "the_persistent_problem": "Traditional software improves as it's used — it stores analytics, usage data, and patterns that become algorithms. Agents of today don't. No matter how great your context engineering or agentic prompt engineering becomes, one massive problem persists: your agents forget, and that means your agents don't learn.",
    "why_existing_tools_fall_short": "Memory files are global forced context that always loads (expertise requires breaking rules when the time is right) and must be manually updated. Prime prompts, sub-agents, and skills are powerful, but they too must be manually updated to steer agents in a new direction. None of them learn on their own."
  },
  "act_learn_reuse": {
    "summary": "The whole pattern boils down to three concrete steps. An agent expert is any agent wired to do all three; miss one and you have a partial expert.",
    "act": "The agent takes a USEFUL action (keyword: useful) — e.g. builds/updates code, or a user views/adds/checks-out a product. In the codebase experts, 'act' = the build step that modifies the source of truth.",
    "learn": "The agent stores new information: the expertise file gets updated. This is what the self-improve prompt does — it syncs the mental model with the ground truth (the code) after a useful action.",
    "reuse": "On the next execution the agent reuses that information directly from its mental model — the question/plan prompts read the expertise file FIRST and validate it against the codebase, so there's no blind searching.",
    "keyword": "useful — experts only learn from useful actions; and 'after your thorough search, there may be nothing to do — this is perfectly acceptable.'",
    "dan_words": "Agent experts have three concrete steps... Act, learn, reuse. Act. First, our agents take a useful action. The keyword there is useful. Then our agents learn and store new information... Then they reuse that information during the next execution directly from that mental model."
  },
  "self_improving_template_meta_prompt": {
    "headline": "An agent expert is a concrete form of a self-improving template meta prompt. Understand meta prompts and you understand agent experts.",
    "meta_prompt": "A prompt that builds other prompts.",
    "template_meta_prompt": "A prompt that builds other prompts with a specific purpose and structure. (A key leverage point of agentic coding introduced in TAC lesson 3.) This is how you teach agents to operate and build as you do.",
    "self_improving_prompt": "A prompt that updates itself, related prompts, or an isolated file with new information to be used during the agent's next execution.",
    "combined": "Put them together — a prompt with a specific purpose/structure that updates an isolated file (the expertise) for next time — and you get a self-improving template meta prompt. That is the agent expert, mechanically.",
    "dan_words": "The agent expert is a concrete form of a self improving template meta prompt. That's a mouthful. Let's break this down because if you understand meta prompts, you will understand agent experts."
  },
  "meta_agentics": {
    "definition": "Meta-agentics = meta prompts, meta agents (sub-agents), and meta skills. Plainly: prompts writing prompts, agents building agents, skills building skills. They are the atoms of the agent expert AND the building blocks of your entire agentic layer.",
    "why_it_matters": "They greatly increase your output as an agentic engineer, with or without agent experts — they let you build more of your agentic layer faster and serve as the foundation for quickly spinning up new agentic layers (the topic of the final AH lesson).",
    "dan_rule": "There is no code base I create that does not have meta agentics. Every codebase must have meta agentics. Always have a stack of these ready to go.",

    },
    "meta_agent": {
      "file": ".claude/agents/meta-agent.md",
      "does": "An agent that generates other agents: takes a description and writes a complete sub-agent config to .claude/agents/<name>.md (real YAML frontmatter, minimal tools, exactly 4 sections). model: opus.",
      "demo_artifact": ".claude/agents/planner.md (a lightweight agent that reads an existing prompt and fires it — it delegates straight to /plan via SlashCommand — so you can scale planning to many agents in parallel)."

    "meta_skill": {
      "file": ".claude/skills/meta-skill/SKILL.md",
      "skill_name_in_frontmatter": "creating-new-skills",
      "does": "A skill that creates new Agent Skills: reads the bundled Anthropic skills docs (docs/*.md) then scaffolds a SKILL.md following best practices (progressive disclosure, gerund naming, third-person description).",
      "demo_artifact": ".claude/skills/start-orchestrator/SKILL.md (turns the manual 'start the orchestrator FE+BE' process into a concrete skill — flags for --cwd/--session, background start commands, and it even opens the UI in Chrome when done)."
    },
    "the_catch": "Meta-agentics ACT but they do not LEARN — nothing inside the meta prompt, meta agent, or meta skill updates automatically; they don't become more proficient over time. Therefore they are NOT agent experts. Agent experts must learn on their own."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agents-forget",
      "name": "The persistent problem: agents forget",
      "plain_english": "Traditional software gets better as people use it (analytics, usage data, patterns → algorithms). Agents don't — they start fresh every session and forget everything. Great context and prompt engineering don't fix this; it's a category problem, and it's the one agent experts exist to solve.",
      "dan_words": "\"Your agents forget. And that means your agents don't learn.\"",
      "misconception": "That better prompts or bigger context windows eventually solve forgetting. They don't — forgetting is structural. What you need is a mechanism that turns actions into stored, reusable expertise."
    },
    {
      "id": "executes-and-learns",
      "name": "Generic agent vs agent expert: forgets vs learns",
      "plain_english": "The entire difference is one word. A generic agent executes and forgets. An agent expert executes and LEARNS. You don't have to tell an expert to learn each time — learning is built into how it operates. Real experts never stop updating their mental model of the one domain that matters most.",
      "dan_words": "\"The difference between a generic agent and an agent expert is simple. One executes and forgets, the other executes and learns... You don't need to tell an expert to learn. It's in their DNA.\"",
      "misconception": "That an 'expert' means a bigger/smarter model or a longer system prompt. No — it's an ordinary agent wired into an Act→Learn→Reuse loop over a persistent mental model. The two experts in this lesson use no custom tools and no specialized system prompt."
    },
    {
      "id": "mental-model",
      "name": "The mental model (a data structure that evolves)",
      "plain_english": "Expertise is a mental model, and a mental model is simply a data structure that evolves over time. With each useful action you accumulate information, examples, and expertise about ONE domain — not every problem, the one that matters to you, your business, your customers. Give your agents the same: an expertise file.",
      "dan_words": "\"This mental model is simply put a data structure that evolves over time... You and everyone you admire has a strong mental model around a specific domain down to individual problems.\"",
      "misconception": "That you should build a general 'know-everything' agent. Experts are narrow by design — you pick the domain (database, websockets, billing) and go deep."
    },
    {
      "id": "not-a-source-of-truth",
      "name": "The expertise file is a mental model, NOT a source of truth",
      "plain_english": "The single most-repeated point: the expertise file is not documentation, not a second source of truth, not a duplicate of the code. It's the agent's working memory — a rough approximation it constantly re-validates. Your mind isn't a source of truth either; it's a mental model you refresh when you dive into an area.",
      "dan_words": "\"This is not a source of truth, okay?... You don't have a source of truth in your mind. You have a working memory file. You have a mental model.\"",
      "misconception": "\"Now I have to maintain the code, the comments, the PRDs, the plans, AND an expertise file — another source of truth to drift.\" No: it's a mental model, the agent maintains it via self-improve, and it always re-validates against the real source of truth."
    },
    {
      "id": "source-of-truth-is-code",
      "name": "The true source of truth is always the code",
      "plain_english": "The mental model is valuable, but the code is what actually runs and builds the product — not the comments, not the docs, not the plans. So every expert prompt reads its expertise FIRST, then validates that mental model against the live codebase before acting or answering.",
      "dan_words": "\"The true source of truth is always the code. You and I know that. Not the comments, not the documentation, not the plans. It is the code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the expertise file can be trusted blindly to save time. It can't — it's a fast index, but the workflow always confirms it against code (that's why 'validate against the codebase' appears twice in the question prompt)."

      "id": "self-improving-template-meta-prompt",
      "name": "Self-improving template meta prompt (the definition)",
      "plain_english": "Meta prompt = a prompt that builds prompts. Template meta prompt = does it with a fixed purpose/structure. Self-improving = updates an isolated file with new info for next time. Combine all three and you have the formal definition of an agent expert.",
      "dan_words": "\"Meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts. Template meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts with a specific purpose and structure... When we put it all together, you get a self-improving template metaprompt.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'meta prompt' is jargon for hype. It's mechanical and concrete: a prompt whose output is another prompt or an updated knowledge file."
    },
    {
      "id": "meta-agentics",
      "name": "Meta-agentics: prompts building prompts, agents building agents, skills building skills",
      "plain_english": "Before experts, learn the building blocks: meta prompts, meta agents, meta skills. They let you produce your agentic layer faster. They ACT (they build things) but they don't LEARN — so they're the atoms of an expert, not experts themselves.",
      "dan_words": "\"There is no code base I create that does not have meta agentics. Every codebase must have meta agentics.\"",
      "misconception": "That meta-agentics are already agent experts because they 'do work.' They're missing the learn step — nothing about them improves automatically."
    },
    {
      "id": "the-act-step-distinguisher",
      "name": "The missing 'act' step: partial expert vs complete expert",
      "plain_english": "The database expert has Reuse (the question prompt) and Learn (self-improve) but NO Act — no prompt that changes code, so nothing new happens to learn from. That's a fine, acceptable partial expert. The websocket expert adds Act (a build step that edits code), which makes it a complete Act→Learn→Reuse expert.",
      "dan_words": "\"Looking at our database expert... We have a reuse step... We also have a learn step... Now, where's our act step? We don't actually have any action prompts here. Nothing is changing.\"",
      "misconception": "That an expert must always modify code. Read-only experts (question/answer over a mental model) are legitimate and useful — they just have reuse+learn without act."
    },
    {
      "id": "self-improve-prompt",
      "name": "The self-improve prompt (the learn mechanism)",
      "plain_english": "A ~99-190 line template meta prompt that keeps the mental model synced with the code: optionally read the git diff, read current expertise, validate against the codebase, list discrepancies, update the file, enforce a hard line limit, and validate the YAML compiles. It's a closed-loop prompt — the agent must know how to manage its own memory.",
      "dan_words": "\"This self improve prompt is telling us that our agents mental model is synced with the ground truth. This is the equivalent of you going to the codebase, refreshing your memory on a feature before you start building.\"",
      "misconception": "That you must prescribe exactly what to store. Dan deliberately doesn't — he seeds loosely and lets the agent define and maintain the structure ('it's their mental model, not yours'), steering toward autonomy."
    },
    {
      "id": "never-edit-expertise-directly",
      "name": "Never hand-edit the expertise file — fix the self-improve step",
      "plain_english": "When the mental model is wrong, the temptation is to open the file and fix it. Don't. Update the self-improve prompt (or the agentics that operate the code) so the agent maintains it correctly. This is the literal act of building the system that builds the system.",
      "dan_words": "\"We're not going to update the expertise file... You wanna update the self-improve step that operates your expertise... Build the system that builds the system. Do not work on the application layer. You're wasting your time.\"",
      "misconception": "That editing the file directly is a harmless shortcut. It quietly returns you to manual memory maintenance — the exact problem experts exist to remove — and doesn't fix the root cause (the learning rubric)."
    },
    {
      "id": "scale-compute-confidence",
      "name": "Scale compute for confidence (deploy N experts)",
      "plain_english": "Because experts are cheap prompts, you can fire the same question at 3, 5, or 10 of them and co-locate on the right answer. More compute = more confidence. Sometimes only one of five completes, or one finds what the others missed, and you compose the results.",
      "dan_words": "\"Instead of having one agent answer something for you, have three, have five, have 10... more compute equals more confidence.\"",
      "misconception": "That parallel experts are wasteful. For high-stakes answers, redundancy is the point — non-deterministic agents surface different evidence; composing them beats a single run."
    },

      "id": "product-agent-experts",
      "name": "Product agent experts (per-user mental models + generative UI)",
      "plain_english": "The same pattern applied to users: a per-user expertise file (viewed / added-to-cart / checked-out) plus a prompt that generates UI on the fly = personalization to the max.       "misconception": "That this demo (Nile) is a production recommendation engine. Dan is explicit it isn't — agents are too slow for that today; it's a rough seed showing the act/learn/reuse pattern inside a product UI."

      "id": "everything-is-the-core-four",

  "quotes": [
    { "text": "This will likely be the most controversial lesson of Agentic Horizon.", "approx_timestamp": "0:11" },
    { "text": "Your agents forget. And that means your agents don't learn.", "approx_timestamp": "0:53" },
    { "text": "The difference between a generic agent and an agent expert is simple. One executes and forgets, the other executes and learns.", "approx_timestamp": "2:02" },
    { "text": "You don't need to tell an expert to learn. It's in their DNA.", "approx_timestamp": "2:18" },
    { "text": "This mental model is a data structure that helps you solve problems better and faster as you act, learn, and reuse that expertise.", "approx_timestamp": "3:11" },
    { "text": "The agent expert is a concrete form of a self improving template meta prompt.", "approx_timestamp": "3:25" },
    { "text": "Meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts. Template meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts with a specific purpose and structure.", "approx_timestamp": "3:39" },
    { "text": "There is no code base I create that does not have meta agentics. Every codebase must have meta agentics.", "approx_timestamp": "7:05" },
    { "text": "This is a key factor of what makes an agent expert, they must learn on their own.", "approx_timestamp": "8:44" },
    { "text": "The expertise file is the mental model of the problem space for your agent expert.", "approx_timestamp": "10:11" },
    { "text": "This is not a source of truth. This is your agent's mental model.", "approx_timestamp": "11:20" },
    { "text": "The true source of truth is always the code. You and I know that. Not the comments, not the documentation, not the plans.", "approx_timestamp": "12:38" },
    { "text": "Give your agents a mental model by giving them an expertise file.", "approx_timestamp": "16:08" },
    { "text": "Once you start building something repeatedly in your system, you wanna move that into automation. Three times marks a pattern. I in fact do have a meta expert.", "approx_timestamp": "28:15" },
    { "text": "Act, learn, reuse. Act. First, our agents take a useful action. The keyword there is useful.", "approx_timestamp": "21:41" },
    { "text": "We can now plan, build and improve anything related to WebSocket functionality in this code base with a single one shot prompt.", "approx_timestamp": "26:31" },
    { "text": "I get super hyped when agents change just the right things. I wanna see surgical changes like this.", "approx_timestamp": "34:53" },
    { "text": "We're not going to update the expertise file. Teach your agents how to directly update it so they can maintain it.", "approx_timestamp": "37:00" },
    { "text": "Build the system that builds the system. Do not work on the application layer. You're wasting your time.", "approx_timestamp": "37:10" },
    { "text": "My Agentic Experts have caught revenue changing details in these systems and security specific details because they were experts.", "approx_timestamp": "40:40" },
    { "text": "As the complexity, as the size of your codebase grows, the agent expert becomes more valuable.", "approx_timestamp": "56:50" },
    { "text": "Do you want a generalist working on your codebase that forgets every time they work? Or do you want an expert that remembers and learns from the work done?", "approx_timestamp": "61:29" },
    { "text": "You and I, the Agentic engineer, we build the system that builds the system.", "approx_timestamp": "62:10" }

    "The expertise file is a MENTAL MODEL, not a source of truth. The code is the only source of truth; every expert prompt re-validates its mental model against the code.",
