  "retrieval_questions": [
    { "q": "What is the one massive problem with today's agents that great context/prompt engineering can't solve?", "a": "They forget, so they don't learn. Traditional software improves with use; agents start cold every time." },
    { "q": "Define an agent expert in one sentence.", "a": "A generic agent wired into an Act → Learn → Reuse loop over a persistent expertise file (mental model) that it maintains itself — it executes and learns, rather than executes and forgets." },
    { "q": "What are the three parts of a 'self-improving template meta prompt'?", "a": "Meta prompt (a prompt that builds prompts) + template (a specific purpose/structure) + self-improving (updates an isolated file with new info for next time)." },
    { "q": "What are the three steps of the pattern, and what's the keyword?", "a": "Act, Learn, Reuse. The keyword is 'useful' — experts learn only from useful actions." },
    { "q": "The database expert is a 'partial' expert. Which step is missing and why?", "a": "The Act step — it has no prompt that modifies code, so nothing changes for it to learn from. It has Reuse (question) and Learn (self-improve) only." },
    { "q": "In the websocket expert, which step maps to plan, build, and self-improve?", "a": "Plan = Reuse (load + validate the mental model), Build = Act (edit the code), Self-improve = Learn (sync the expertise to the git diff)." },
    { "q": "Is the expertise file a source of truth? What is?", "a": "No — it's a mental model. The code is the only source of truth; the expert re-validates its mental model against the code every time." },
    { "q": "The mental model is wrong. What do you change — and what do you NOT change?", "a": "Change the self-improve prompt (or the agentics operating the code). Do NOT hand-edit the expertise file — that returns you to manual memory maintenance and skips the root cause." },
    { "q": "How is the finite-context problem handled?", "a": "A hard MAX_LINES (1000) declared in the self-improve prompt and enforced by the agent on itself (wc -l, trim least-critical), keeping the file well under ~1000 lines." },
    { "q": "Name three great places to build a codebase expert and one place not to.", "a": "Build: billing, security, database (also DevOps, integrations, ML, API, data-types-in-sync). Don't: static/unchanging problems (also simple/new codebases, or areas where you lack a mental model)." },
    { "q": "What is 'seeding' and how does Dan recommend doing it?", "a": "Creating the first version of the expertise. Stay hands-off: run self-improve from blank, let the agent define the structure, tweak the self-improve prompt, and rerun until the agent stops finding new things." },
    { "q": "In the Nile product expert, what is the per-user 'mental model' and how does Act/Learn/Reuse show up?", "a": "A per-user expertise (viewed/added-to-cart/checked-out, stored as JSON).     { "q": "Why deploy three (or five) experts on the same question?", "a": "More compute = more confidence. Non-deterministic agents surface different evidence; sometimes only one completes or finds the missing detail, and you compose the results." },
    { "q": "Meta-agentics act — why aren't they agent experts?", "a": "They don't learn: nothing in the meta prompt/agent/skill updates automatically or gets more proficient over time." }

  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agents-forget",
      "name": "The persistent problem: agents forget",
      "plain_english": "Traditional software gets better as people use it (analytics, usage data, patterns → algorithms). Agents don't — they start fresh every session and forget everything. Great context and prompt engineering don't fix this; it's a category problem, and it's the one agent experts exist to solve.",
      "dan_words": "\"Your agents forget. And that means your agents don't learn.\"",
      "misconception": "That better prompts or bigger context windows eventually solve forgetting. They don't — forgetting is structural. What you need is a mechanism that turns actions into stored, reusable expertise."
    },
    {
      "id": "executes-and-learns",
      "name": "Generic agent vs agent expert: forgets vs learns",
      "plain_english": "The entire difference is one word. A generic agent executes and forgets. An agent expert executes and LEARNS. You don't have to tell an expert to learn each time — learning is built into how it operates. Real experts never stop updating their mental model of the one domain that matters most.",
      "dan_words": "\"The difference between a generic agent and an agent expert is simple. One executes and forgets, the other executes and learns... You don't need to tell an expert to learn. It's in their DNA.\"",
      "misconception": "That an 'expert' means a bigger/smarter model or a longer system prompt. No — it's an ordinary agent wired into an Act→Learn→Reuse loop over a persistent mental model. The two experts in this lesson use no custom tools and no specialized system prompt."
    },
    {
      "id": "mental-model",
      "name": "The mental model (a data structure that evolves)",
      "plain_english": "Expertise is a mental model, and a mental model is simply a data structure that evolves over time. With each useful action you accumulate information, examples, and expertise about ONE domain — not every problem, the one that matters to you, your business, your customers. Give your agents the same: an expertise file.",
      "dan_words": "\"This mental model is simply put a data structure that evolves over time... You and everyone you admire has a strong mental model around a specific domain down to individual problems.\"",
      "misconception": "That you should build a general 'know-everything' agent. Experts are narrow by design — you pick the domain (database, websockets, billing) and go deep."
    },
    {
      "id": "not-a-source-of-truth",
      "name": "The expertise file is a mental model, NOT a source of truth",
      "plain_english": "The single most-repeated point: the expertise file is not documentation, not a second source of truth, not a duplicate of the code. It's the agent's working memory — a rough approximation it constantly re-validates. Your mind isn't a source of truth either; it's a mental model you refresh when you dive into an area.",
      "dan_words": "\"This is not a source of truth, okay?... You don't have a source of truth in your mind. You have a working memory file. You have a mental model.\"",
      "misconception": "\"Now I have to maintain the code, the comments, the PRDs, the plans, AND an expertise file — another source of truth to drift.\" No: it's a mental model, the agent maintains it via self-improve, and it always re-validates against the real source of truth."
    },
    {
      "id": "source-of-truth-is-code",
      "name": "The true source of truth is always the code",
      "plain_english": "The mental model is valuable, but the code is what actually runs and builds the product — not the comments, not the docs, not the plans. So every expert prompt reads its expertise FIRST, then validates that mental model against the live codebase before acting or answering.",
      "dan_words": "\"The true source of truth is always the code. You and I know that. Not the comments, not the documentation, not the plans. It is the code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the expertise file can be trusted blindly to save time. It can't — it's a fast index, but the workflow always confirms it against code (that's why 'validate against the codebase' appears twice in the question prompt)."
    },
    {
      "id": "self-improving-template-meta-prompt",
      "name": "Self-improving template meta prompt (the definition)",
      "plain_english": "Meta prompt = a prompt that builds prompts. Template meta prompt = does it with a fixed purpose/structure. Self-improving = updates an isolated file with new info for next time. Combine all three and you have the formal definition of an agent expert.",
      "dan_words": "\"Meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts. Template meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts with a specific purpose and structure... When we put it all together, you get a self-improving template metaprompt.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'meta prompt' is jargon for hype. It's mechanical and concrete: a prompt whose output is another prompt or an updated knowledge file."
    },
    {
      "id": "meta-agentics",
      "name": "Meta-agentics: prompts building prompts, agents building agents, skills building skills",
      "plain_english": "Before experts, learn the building blocks: meta prompts, meta agents, meta skills. They let you produce your agentic layer faster. They ACT (they build things) but they don't LEARN — so they're the atoms of an expert, not experts themselves.",
      "dan_words": "\"There is no code base I create that does not have meta agentics. Every codebase must have meta agentics.\"",
      "misconception": "That meta-agentics are already agent experts because they 'do work.' They're missing the learn step — nothing about them improves automatically."
    },
    {
      "id": "the-act-step-distinguisher",
      "name": "The missing 'act' step: partial expert vs complete expert",
      "plain_english": "The database expert has Reuse (the question prompt) and Learn (self-improve) but NO Act — no prompt that changes code, so nothing new happens to learn from. That's a fine, acceptable partial expert. The websocket expert adds Act (a build step that edits code), which makes it a complete Act→Learn→Reuse expert.",
      "dan_words": "\"Looking at our database expert... We have a reuse step... We also have a learn step... Now, where's our act step? We don't actually have any action prompts here. Nothing is changing.\"",
      "misconception": "That an expert must always modify code. Read-only experts (question/answer over a mental model) are legitimate and useful — they just have reuse+learn without act."
    },
    {
      "id": "self-improve-prompt",
      "name": "The self-improve prompt (the learn mechanism)",
      "plain_english": "A ~99-190 line template meta prompt that keeps the mental model synced with the code: optionally read the git diff, read current expertise, validate against the codebase, list discrepancies, update the file, enforce a hard line limit, and validate the YAML compiles. It's a closed-loop prompt — the agent must know how to manage its own memory.",
      "dan_words": "\"This self improve prompt is telling us that our agents mental model is synced with the ground truth. This is the equivalent of you going to the codebase, refreshing your memory on a feature before you start building.\"",
      "misconception": "That you must prescribe exactly what to store. Dan deliberately doesn't — he seeds loosely and lets the agent define and maintain the structure ('it's their mental model, not yours'), steering toward autonomy."
    },
    {
      "id": "never-edit-expertise-directly",
      "name": "Never hand-edit the expertise file — fix the self-improve step",
      "plain_english": "When the mental model is wrong, the temptation is to open the file and fix it. Don't. Update the self-improve prompt (or the agentics that operate the code) so the agent maintains it correctly. This is the literal act of building the system that builds the system.",
      "dan_words": "\"We're not going to update the expertise file... You wanna update the self-improve step that operates your expertise... Build the system that builds the system. Do not work on the application layer. You're wasting your time.\"",
      "misconception": "That editing the file directly is a harmless shortcut. It quietly returns you to manual memory maintenance — the exact problem experts exist to remove — and doesn't fix the root cause (the learning rubric)."
    },
    {
      "id": "scale-compute-confidence",
      "name": "Scale compute for confidence (deploy N experts)",
      "plain_english": "Because experts are cheap prompts, you can fire the same question at 3, 5, or 10 of them and co-locate on the right answer. More compute = more confidence. Sometimes only one of five completes, or one finds what the others missed, and you compose the results.",
      "dan_words": "\"Instead of having one agent answer something for you, have three, have five, have 10... more compute equals more confidence.\"",
      "misconception": "That parallel experts are wasteful. For high-stakes answers, redundancy is the point — non-deterministic agents surface different evidence; composing them beats a single run."
    },
    {
      "id": "product-agent-experts",
      "name": "Product agent experts (per-user mental models + generative UI)",
      "plain_english": "The same pattern applied to users: a per-user expertise file (viewed / added-to-cart / checked-out) plus a prompt that generates UI on the fly = personalization to the max. When a user acts, the agent learns; on the next page it reuses to stream an adaptive experience. A seed of a whole new product class.",
      "dan_words": "\"user-specific data, right, down to that action level, so that when they act, your agent learns, and then it reuses to enhance the experience... This is personalization to the max, especially when you combine that with generative UI.\"",
      "misconception": "That this demo (Nile) is a production recommendation engine. Dan is explicit it isn't — agents are too slow for that today; it's a rough seed showing the act/learn/reuse pattern inside a product UI."
    },
    {
      "id": "everything-is-the-core-four",
      "name": "Every abstraction boils down to the core four",
      "plain_english": "Skill, sub-agent, MCP server, custom system prompt — build whatever abstraction fits you and your team. Underneath, an agent expert is still just context, model, prompt, tools with a little tooling and structure. Stay close to bare metal; don't let a new pattern get tangled in other abstractions.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything becomes the core four. Context, model, prompt, tools. Every abstraction on top of that... It's just that. It's an abstraction. It boils down to the same thing.\"",
      "misconception": "That you must pick the 'right' container (skill vs agent vs MCP) for an expert. It doesn't matter — they all reduce to the core four; choose by ergonomics (e.g. sub-agent to parallelize)."
    }
  ],

    "The problem is structural: agents forget, therefore they don't learn. Better prompts/context don't fix it — a self-improving loop does.",
    "An agent expert = a generic agent wired into Act → Learn → Reuse over a persistent expertise file. No special model, system prompt, or tools required.",
    "Mechanically, an agent expert is a self-improving template meta prompt: a structured prompt that updates an isolated knowledge file for next time.",
    "The expertise file is a MENTAL MODEL, not a source of truth. The code is the only source of truth; every expert prompt re-validates its mental model against the code.",
    "Reuse = read expertise first, validate vs code, then answer/plan. Learn = self-improve syncs the file to the code. Act = a build step that changes the code (the piece a 'partial' expert lacks).",
    "Never hand-edit the expertise file — fix the self-improve prompt so the agent maintains it. That IS building the system that builds the system.",
    "Seed loosely and let the agent own its data structure; enforce a hard line limit; expect and design for false expertise.",
    "Build experts for high-risk/high-complexity/high-error areas (billing, security, database, integrations) and for per-user product experiences — not for static, simple, or brand-new code, and not for areas where you lack a mental model.",

  "teach_back_prompt": "Explain to a teammate, without notes: (1) why agents 'forgetting' is a structural problem that context/prompt engineering can't fix, and what an agent expert adds; (2) the exact definition of a self-improving template meta prompt, and map its three parts onto Act/Learn/Reuse; (3) using the database vs websocket experts, show which one is 'partial' and why — name the missing step and what supplies it; (4) why the expertise file is a mental model and NOT a source of truth, and what the agent validates it against; and (5) why you fix the self-improve prompt instead of hand-editing the expertise file. Finish by naming two systems in your own codebase where you'd build an expert — and one where you wouldn't — with the reason for each.",
  "retrieval_questions": [
    { "q": "What is the one massive problem with today's agents that great context/prompt engineering can't solve?", "a": "They forget, so they don't learn. Traditional software improves with use; agents start cold every time." },
    { "q": "Define an agent expert in one sentence.", "a": "A generic agent wired into an Act → Learn → Reuse loop over a persistent expertise file (mental model) that it maintains itself — it executes and learns, rather than executes and forgets." },
    { "q": "What are the three parts of a 'self-improving template meta prompt'?", "a": "Meta prompt (a prompt that builds prompts) + template (a specific purpose/structure) + self-improving (updates an isolated file with new info for next time)." },
    { "q": "What are the three steps of the pattern, and what's the keyword?", "a": "Act, Learn, Reuse. The keyword is 'useful' — experts learn only from useful actions." },
    { "q": "The database expert is a 'partial' expert. Which step is missing and why?", "a": "The Act step — it has no prompt that modifies code, so nothing changes for it to learn from. It has Reuse (question) and Learn (self-improve) only." },
    { "q": "In the websocket expert, which step maps to plan, build, and self-improve?", "a": "Plan = Reuse (load + validate the mental model), Build = Act (edit the code), Self-improve = Learn (sync the expertise to the git diff)." },
    { "q": "Is the expertise file a source of truth? What is?", "a": "No — it's a mental model. The code is the only source of truth; the expert re-validates its mental model against the code every time." },
    { "q": "The mental model is wrong. What do you change — and what do you NOT change?", "a": "Change the self-improve prompt (or the agentics operating the code). Do NOT hand-edit the expertise file — that returns you to manual memory maintenance and skips the root cause." },
    { "q": "How is the finite-context problem handled?", "a": "A hard MAX_LINES (1000) declared in the self-improve prompt and enforced by the agent on itself (wc -l, trim least-critical), keeping the file well under ~1000 lines." },
    { "q": "Name three great places to build a codebase expert and one place not to.", "a": "Build: billing, security, database (also DevOps, integrations, ML, API, data-types-in-sync). Don't: static/unchanging problems (also simple/new codebases, or areas where you lack a mental model)." },
    { "q": "What is 'seeding' and how does Dan recommend doing it?", "a": "Creating the first version of the expertise. Stay hands-off: run self-improve from blank, let the agent define the structure, tweak the self-improve prompt, and rerun until the agent stops finding new things." },
    { "q": "In the Nile product expert, what is the per-user 'mental model' and how does Act/Learn/Reuse show up?", "a": "A per-user expertise (viewed/added-to-cart/checked-out, stored as JSON). Act = user browses/buys; Learn = the action is recorded; Reuse = the home page regenerates a personalized, streamed generative UI." },
    { "q": "Why deploy three (or five) experts on the same question?", "a": "More compute = more confidence. Non-deterministic agents surface different evidence; sometimes only one completes or finds the missing detail, and you compose the results." },
    { "q": "Meta-agentics act — why aren't they agent experts?", "a": "They don't learn: nothing in the meta prompt/agent/skill updates automatically or gets more proficient over time." }
  ],

# AH-5 "Agent Experts" — master teaching notes

> Lesson 13 of the course, lesson 5 of Agentic Horizon. Runtime 62:29. The self-described "most controversial lesson of Agentic Horizon."
>
> **One line:** stop deploying agents that *execute and forget*; wire them into an **Act → Learn → Reuse** loop over a self-maintained **expertise file** (a mental model) so each useful action becomes reusable expertise — with no human in the loop.

Each major idea below follows the same weak-student scaffold: **Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name it (Dan's words) → Failure mode → Retrieval.** Quotes are VTT-verified; timestamps are ±3s.

---

## Idea 1 — The problem is structural: agents forget

**Hook.** You already know agents are forgetful. What you may not have named is *why it's fatal*: normal software gets **better** the more it's used (analytics, usage data, patterns → algorithms). Your agents get exactly as good on run #1000 as on run #1.

**Picture.** Two staircases. Traditional software climbs with usage. Agents flatline — every session starts at the bottom.

**Worked example.** No matter how good your context engineering or agentic prompt engineering gets, a fresh agent pointed at your billing code re-derives the same understanding from scratch, every time, and throws it away when the session ends.

**Name it.** *"Your agents forget. And that means your agents don't learn."* (0:53) The existing tools don't close the gap: **memory files** are global forced context that always loads (and expertise needs to break rules when the time is right) and must be updated by hand; **prime prompts, sub-agents, skills** are powerful but also hand-updated.

**Failure mode.** Believing a bigger context window or a cleverer prompt eventually fixes forgetting. It can't — forgetting is structural. You need a mechanism that *stores* what was learned.

**Retrieval.** What's the one problem great context/prompt engineering can't solve, and why does it matter more than it sounds?

---

## Idea 2 — The fix is one word: **learns**

**Hook.** The whole difference between a generic agent and an expert fits in a single verb.

**Picture.** Same agent, two wirings. Left: `execute → forget`. Right: `execute → learn → (next time) start smarter`.

**Worked example.** Both experts Dan builds use **no custom tools and no specialized system prompt**. They're ordinary agents — the difference is the loop they're wired into.

**Name it.** *"One executes and forgets, the other executes and learns... You don't need to tell an expert to learn. It's in their DNA."* (2:02) Real experts never stop updating their mental model of the **one** domain that matters most to them.

**Failure mode.** Thinking "expert" means a smarter/bigger model or a longer prompt. It means a persistent, self-maintained mental model plus a loop.

**Retrieval.** Define an agent expert in one sentence without using the words "smart" or "model."

---

## Idea 3 — Expertise is a **mental model**, not a source of truth

**Hook.** The instant you propose an expertise file, a good engineer objects: "great, *another* source of truth to drift — code, comments, PRDs, plans, and now this?"

**Picture.** Your own head. You don't carry a source of truth in there; you carry a fuzzy, self-updating **mental model** you refresh when you dive into an area. The file is the agent's version of that.

**Worked example.** The database expert's `expertise.yaml` says "Postgres + asyncpg, lightweight Pydantic over raw SQL, idempotent migrations, 6 tables." That's an *approximation* — a fast index — that the agent re-checks against the code before trusting it.

**Name it.** *"This is not a source of truth. This is your agent's mental model."* (11:20) And its complement: *"The true source of truth is always the code... Not the comments, not the documentation, not the plans."* (12:38)

**Failure mode.** Two symmetrical errors: (a) distrusting the file as "duplicate docs," or (b) trusting it blindly to save time. Correct stance: it's a mental model the agent **always re-validates against code** (that's why "validate against the codebase" appears *twice* in the question prompt).

**Retrieval.** Is the expertise file a source of truth? What is, and what does the expert do with the file before answering?

---

## Idea 4 — The mechanism: a **self-improving template meta prompt**

**Hook.** Dan gives the whole thing a mouthful of a name, then insists it's simple once you decompose it.

**Picture.** Three Lego bricks snapping together: `[meta prompt] + [template] + [self-improving] = agent expert`.

**Worked example.**
- **Meta prompt** = a prompt that builds other prompts. (`meta_prompt.md` writes new slash commands.)
- **Template** meta prompt = does it with a fixed **purpose and structure**. (TAC-3's leverage point.)
- **Self-improving** = updates an isolated file with new info **for next time**.
- Combine them and you have the formal definition of an agent expert.

**Name it.** *"The agent expert is a concrete form of a self improving template meta prompt... Meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts. Template meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts with a specific purpose and structure."* (3:25–3:39)

**Failure mode.** Hearing "meta prompt" as hype. It's mechanical: a prompt whose **output is another prompt or an updated knowledge file**.

**Retrieval.** Name the three parts of a self-improving template meta prompt.

---

## Idea 5 — Meta-agentics: the building blocks (that act but don't learn)

**Hook.** Before experts, Dan builds the *atoms* — and shows you a trap.

**Picture.** Three factories: prompts building prompts, agents building agents, skills building skills. All three ship a product; none of them get better on their own.

**Worked example (all three demoed live and shipped to the repo):**
- **Meta prompt** → `question-w-mermaid-diagrams.md` (a question prompt that always adds mermaid). *[frame t0456]*
- **Meta agent** → `planner.md` (reads an existing prompt and fires it as a sub-agent via `/plan` — so planning scales to many parallel agents).
- **Meta skill** → `start-orchestrator/SKILL.md` (boots the app's front+back end and opens Chrome). *[frame t0508]*

**Name it.** *"There is no code base I create that does not have meta agentics. Every codebase must have meta agentics."* (7:05)

**Failure mode / the trap.** Concluding these are already experts because they "do work." *"They're acting but... they're not learning at all. Nothing... has updated automatically... therefore these are not Agentic Experts."* (8:36) **Agent experts must learn on their own.**

**Retrieval.** Meta-agentics *act*. Why aren't they experts?

---

## Idea 6 — The pattern: **Act · Learn · Reuse** *(the one to memorize)*

**Hook.** Everything collapses to three steps. *[frame t1305 — the branded Act/Learn/Reuse graphic over a real expert prompt]*

**Picture.** A loop: **Act** (☀ take a useful action) → **Learn** (🧠 store new info) → **Reuse** (🔁 pull from the mental model next time) → back to Act.

**Worked example.** Watch which files supply which step (see Idea 9). The keyword is **useful** — and its honest twin: *"after your thorough search, there may be nothing to be done — this is perfectly acceptable."*

**Name it.** *"Act, learn, reuse. Act. First, our agents take a useful action. The keyword there is useful."* (21:41)

**Failure mode.** Building only Reuse + Learn and expecting compounding gains — without an **Act** step there's no useful action to learn from (that's the "partial expert" trap in Idea 9).

**Retrieval.** Three steps, and the keyword? What's the "perfectly acceptable" outcome of a learn pass?

---

## Idea 7 — The expertise file: anatomy of a mental model

**Hook.** "What's actually *in* one of these?" *[frame t2182 — the 677-line websocket file, collapsed to its spine]*

**Picture.** A YAML outline with exact `file:line` references, e.g. `overview → core_implementation → event_types → streaming_architecture → … → architecture_summary`.

**Worked example.** The database file's `session_state.websocketEventCount` entry (in the websocket file) records `lines: "78"`, `reset_on: connect (line 388), disconnect (line 409)`. Dan notes the database file has *"44 instances of specific line numbers"* — so the agent can jump straight to code and re-validate fast.

**Name it.** *"Give your agents a mental model by giving them an expertise file."* (16:08) Format is your choice — Dan likes YAML but says TOML/JSON/CSV/DB-JSONB all work; pick what's easiest for your agents to read.

**Failure mode.** Letting it grow forever. A hard `MAX_LINES: 1000` lives in the self-improve prompt and the agent enforces it on itself (`wc -l`, then trim least-critical). Dan stays under ~1000 lines.

**Retrieval.** What keeps an expertise file from bloating, and why does it carry exact line numbers?

---

## Idea 8 — The self-improve prompt: the **Learn** mechanism (and the golden rule)

**Hook.** How does a file "improve itself"? It doesn't — a prompt improves it. *[frame t1255 — self-improve.md workflow]*

**Picture.** A closed loop: `(git diff) → read current expertise → validate vs codebase → list discrepancies → update → enforce line limit → validate YAML compiles`.

**Worked example.** Run `/experts:database:self-improve`. The agent burns top-to-bottom, checks line count, compiles the YAML (`python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(...)"`), and reports discrepancies — or reports there was nothing to do and stops. Dan seeds **loosely** and lets the agent define its own structure ("it's their mental model, not yours").

**Name it (the golden rule).** *"We're not going to update the expertise file... Teach your agents how to directly update it so they can maintain it."* (37:00) → *"Build the system that builds the system. Do not work on the application layer. You're wasting your time."* (37:10)

**Failure mode.** Hand-editing the expertise file when it's wrong. It feels harmless, but it quietly restores manual memory maintenance — the exact problem experts remove — and never fixes the root cause: the **self-improve prompt**.

**Retrieval.** The mental model is wrong. What do you change, and what do you refuse to touch?

---

## Idea 9 — Partial vs complete expert: the **missing Act step**

**Hook.** Dan shows a *partial* expert first — on purpose.

**Picture.** A checklist per expert: `[Act] [Learn] [Reuse]`.

**Worked example.**
| | Database expert | WebSocket expert |
|---|---|---|
| **Reuse** | `question.md` (read expertise → validate → answer; **read-only**) | `plan.md` / `question.md` |
| **Learn** | `self-improve.md` | `self-improve.md` (run with `true` → reads the git diff) |
| **Act** | ❌ none — no prompt changes code | ✅ `build.md` edits real code |
| **Orchestration** | — | `plan_build_improve.md` chains all three *[frame t1598]* |

The database expert is *"completely acceptable"* — a fine partial. The websocket expert adds the Act step (build a session-based nav-bar WebSocket counter), completing the loop.

**Name it.** *"Now, where's our act step? We don't actually have any action prompts here. Nothing is changing."* (22:20) → the missing act = *"updating any code related to the database."*

**Failure mode.** Assuming an expert must always modify code. Read-only experts (Q&A over a mental model) are legitimate — they just run Reuse + Learn without Act.

**Retrieval.** Which step does the database expert lack, and what supplies it in the websocket expert?

---

## Idea 10 — Context delegation & "more compute = more confidence"

**Hook.** A complete expert runs a lot of tokens. How does the top agent not drown?

**Picture.** A conductor (top agent) firing three fresh musicians (sub-agents), each handed only what they need, handing back only a summary. *[frame t2019 — three Task blocks with token stats]*

**Worked example.** `plan_build_improve.md` spawns three `Task` sub-agents in sequence — **plan (81.8k tokens) → build (61.4k tokens, 41 tool uses) → self-improve** — each starting fresh, so the top agent's context stays protected; it just passes the plan into the builder and the git diff into self-improve. Separately, Dan fires the *same* websocket question at **three** experts to co-locate on the answer; websocket-3 fails — and that's the point.

**Name it.** *"Instead of having one agent answer something for you, have three, have five, have 10... more compute equals more confidence."* (25:00) Ties back to TAC-6: **one agent, one prompt, one purpose** — even inside a scaled workflow.

**Failure mode.** Reading parallel experts as waste. For high-stakes answers, redundancy surfaces evidence a single run misses; you compose the survivors.

**Retrieval.** Why isolate plan/build/self-improve into separate sub-agents? Why fire three experts at one question?

---

## Idea 11 — Product agent experts: per-user mental models + generative UI

**Hook.** Point the same pattern at *users* instead of code and you get a seed of a new product class. *[frames t2545 → t2588, a before/after]*

**Picture.** One expertise file **per user**: `{viewed_products, added_to_cart, checked_out}` → a prompt that streams UI components on the fly.

**Worked example (Nile).** New user, empty expertise → **generic** "Welcome to Nile." Dan searches "Nvidia DGX," adds to cart (an **Act**), returns → the agent **learned** and **reused**: "Welcome back! Based on your interest in AI workstations," streaming a personalized "Complete Your AI Workstation" carousel. The system prompt exposes dynamic vars (checked-out/added/viewed products) and static vars (`SECTIONS_RANGE 4-6`, `PRODUCTS_PER_SECTION_RANGE 6-12`); it's driven by the **Claude Agent SDK** (`agent_expert.py`), and Dan drops Opus→Haiku for speed on camera.

**Name it.** *"when they act, your agent learns, and then it reuses to enhance the experience... This is personalization to the max, especially when you combine that with generative UI."* (42:xx)

**Failure mode.** Mistaking this for a production recommendation engine. Dan is explicit: **it isn't** — agents are too slow for that today; study the *pattern in a UI*, and note the "UI hacks" (loading bars, streamed sections) needed to mask latency.

**Retrieval.** In Nile, what's the per-user mental model, and where do Act/Learn/Reuse show up in the shopping flow?

---

## Idea 12 — When to build an expert (and when NOT to)

**Hook.** The scary insight: build these in your *highest-stakes* code, not your safest.

**Picture.** A 2×2 — risk/complexity vs how-much-it-changes. Experts belong top-right; generic agents belong bottom-left.

**Worked example — build one for:** billing (Dan builds none without an expert; they've *"caught revenue changing details"*), security, the database, DevOps, tricky 3–4-way integrations, ML/data-science, APIs, and **data-types-kept-in-sync** across microservices (a great *first* expert — few files to reference). *"As the complexity, as the size of your codebase grows, the agent expert becomes more valuable."* (56:50)

**Don't build one when:** the problem doesn't evolve; the codebase is simple or brand-new (the model has seen its shape); or **you** don't have a mental model of the area — *"If you don't understand the problem, do not build an Agentic expert... It'll make your problems worse, not better."*

**Failure modes / trade-offs to expect (48:09–53:45):** *seeding* (start blank, let the agent define structure, rerun until it stops finding things), the *"another source of truth"* reflex (it's a mental model — invest in teaching your agents), *finite context* (max-line limit), *false expertise* (agents err like we do — expect it), *too-granular* expertise (a prompt-engineering fix: "prioritize actionable, high-value expertise over verbose documentation"), and *too many experts* (routers/reminders; habit: read the expertise file before working an area).

**Name it (the close).** *"Do you want a generalist working on your codebase that forgets every time they work? Or do you want an expert that remembers and learns from the work done?"* (61:29)

**Retrieval.** Name three build-it domains and one don't-build case. What's the risk of building an expert for a domain you don't understand?

---

## VTT-verified timeline map

| Time | Beat |
|---|---|
| 0:11–3:25 | Controversy framing → the massive problem (forget→don't learn) → generic vs expert → mental model → self-improving template meta prompt (definition) |
| 3:25–5:41 | Definition wrap; experts are "always learning"; lesson roadmap (meta-agentics → codebase experts → product experts) |
| 5:41–8:36 | **Meta-agentics** built + reviewed: meta prompt→question-w-mermaid, meta agent→planner, meta skill→start-orchestrator |
| 8:36–9:00 | They act but don't learn ⇒ not experts |
| 9:32–16:10 | **Database (partial) expert:** experts dir → `/question` reads expertise then validates code → ER-diagram report → expertise.yaml anatomy |
| 16:10–21:05 | **self-improve** run + walkthrough (the Learn rubric); seeding loosely; 44 line-refs |
| 21:40–23:52 | Act/Learn/Reuse defined; database = partial (no Act); the missing act = editing code |
| 23:52–34:25 | **WebSocket (complete) expert:** `/plan build improve` fires → scale to 3 experts → plan_build_improve composition → pipeline metrics (81.8k/61.4k) → counter shows ~167 |
| 34:25–38:20 | Surgical diff; git diff of expertise; **never edit the file — fix self-improve**; lock in Act/Learn/Reuse |
| 38:20–40:30 | Favorite codebase experts (billing/security/db/…); these two are simple (no custom tools/system prompt) |
| 40:30–47:20 | **Product experts (Nile):** per-user expertise, Control-K panel, act→personalized generative UI, system-prompt variables |
| 47:20–53:45 | Challenges & trade-offs (seeding, source-of-truth, finite context, false expertise, granularity, too-many) |
| 53:45–59:20 | When to use / when NOT to |
| 59:20–62:29 | Everything is the core four; generalist-vs-expert close; AH-6 teaser (codebase architecture) |

---

## Glossary (say these back cold)

- **Agent expert** — a generic agent wired into Act→Learn→Reuse over a persistent expertise file it maintains itself.
- **Expertise file** — the agent's mental model of one domain (Dan: YAML); NOT documentation, NOT a source of truth.
- **Mental model** — a data structure that evolves with each useful action; re-validated against the code.
- **Self-improving template meta prompt** — meta prompt (builds prompts) + template (fixed purpose/structure) + self-improving (updates an isolated file for next time).
- **Meta-agentics** — meta prompts / meta agents / meta skills; they act but don't learn.

# AH-5 "Agent Experts" — master teaching notes

> Lesson 13 of the course, lesson 5 of Agentic Horizon. Runtime 62:29. The self-described "most controversial lesson of Agentic Horizon."
>
> **One line:** stop deploying agents that *execute and forget*; wire them into an **Act → Learn → Reuse** loop over a self-maintained **expertise file** (a mental model) so each useful action becomes reusable expertise — with no human in the loop.

Each major idea below follows the same weak-student scaffold: **Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name it (Dan's words) → Failure mode → Retrieval.** Quotes are VTT-verified; timestamps are ±3s.

---

## Idea 1 — The problem is structural: agents forget

**Hook.** You already know agents are forgetful. What you may not have named is *why it's fatal*: normal software gets **better** the more it's used (analytics, usage data, patterns → algorithms). Your agents get exactly as good on run #1000 as on run #1.

**Picture.** Two staircases. Traditional software climbs with usage. Agents flatline — every session starts at the bottom.

**Worked example.** No matter how good your context engineering or agentic prompt engineering gets, a fresh agent pointed at your billing code re-derives the same understanding from scratch, every time, and throws it away when the session ends.

**Name it.** *"Your agents forget. And that means your agents don't learn."* (0:53) The existing tools don't close the gap: **memory files** are global forced context that always loads (and expertise needs to break rules when the time is right) and must be updated by hand; **prime prompts, sub-agents, skills** are powerful but also hand-updated.

**Failure mode.** Believing a bigger context window or a cleverer prompt eventually fixes forgetting. It can't — forgetting is structural. You need a mechanism that *stores* what was learned.

**Retrieval.** What's the one problem great context/prompt engineering can't solve, and why does it matter more than it sounds?

---

## Idea 2 — The fix is one word: **learns**

**Hook.** The whole difference between a generic agent and an expert fits in a single verb.

**Picture.** Same agent, two wirings. Left: `execute → forget`. Right: `execute → learn → (next time) start smarter`.

**Worked example.** Both experts Dan builds use **no custom tools and no specialized system prompt**. They're ordinary agents — the difference is the loop they're wired into.

**Name it.** *"One executes and forgets, the other executes and learns... You don't need to tell an expert to learn. It's in their DNA."* (2:02) Real experts never stop updating their mental model of the **one** domain that matters most to them.

**Failure mode.** Thinking "expert" means a smarter/bigger model or a longer prompt. It means a persistent, self-maintained mental model plus a loop.

**Retrieval.** Define an agent expert in one sentence without using the words "smart" or "model."

---

## Idea 3 — Expertise is a **mental model**, not a source of truth

**Hook.** The instant you propose an expertise file, a good engineer objects: "great, *another* source of truth to drift — code, comments, PRDs, plans, and now this?"

**Picture.** Your own head. You don't carry a source of truth in there; you carry a fuzzy, self-updating **mental model** you refresh when you dive into an area. The file is the agent's version of that.

**Worked example.** The database expert's `expertise.yaml` says "Postgres + asyncpg, lightweight Pydantic over raw SQL, idempotent migrations, 6 tables." That's an *approximation* — a fast index — that the agent re-checks against the code before trusting it.

**Name it.** *"This is not a source of truth. This is your agent's mental model."* (11:20) And its complement: *"The true source of truth is always the code... Not the comments, not the documentation, not the plans."* (12:38)

**Failure mode.** Two symmetrical errors: (a) distrusting the file as "duplicate docs," or (b) trusting it blindly to save time. Correct stance: it's a mental model the agent **always re-validates against code** (that's why "validate against the codebase" appears *twice* in the question prompt).

**Retrieval.** Is the expertise file a source of truth? What is, and what does the expert do with the file before answering?

---

## Idea 4 — The mechanism: a **self-improving template meta prompt**

**Hook.** Dan gives the whole thing a mouthful of a name, then insists it's simple once you decompose it.

**Picture.** Three Lego bricks snapping together: `[meta prompt] + [template] + [self-improving] = agent expert`.

**Worked example.**
- **Meta prompt** = a prompt that builds other prompts. (`meta_prompt.md` writes new slash commands.)
- **Template** meta prompt = does it with a fixed **purpose and structure**. (TAC-3's leverage point.)
- **Self-improving** = updates an isolated file with new info **for next time**.
- Combine them and you have the formal definition of an agent expert.

**Name it.** *"The agent expert is a concrete form of a self improving template meta prompt... Meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts. Template meta prompts are prompts that build other prompts with a specific purpose and structure."* (3:25–3:39)

**Failure mode.** Hearing "meta prompt" as hype. It's mechanical: a prompt whose **output is another prompt or an updated knowledge file**.

**Retrieval.** Name the three parts of a self-improving template meta prompt.

---

## Idea 5 — Meta-agentics: the building blocks (that act but don't learn)

**Hook.** Before experts, Dan builds the *atoms* — and shows you a trap.

**Picture.** Three factories: prompts building prompts, agents building agents, skills building skills. All three ship a product; none of them get better on their own.

**Worked example (all three demoed live and shipped to the repo):**
- **Meta prompt** → `question-w-mermaid-diagrams.md` (a question prompt that always adds mermaid). *[frame t0456]*
- **Meta agent** → `planner.md` (reads an existing prompt and fires it as a sub-agent via `/plan` — so planning scales to many parallel agents).
- **Meta skill** → `start-orchestrator/SKILL.md` (boots the app's front+back end and opens Chrome). *[frame t0508]*

**Name it.** *"There is no code base I create that does not have meta agentics. Every codebase must have meta agentics."* (7:05)

**Failure mode / the trap.** Concluding these are already experts because they "do work." *"They're acting but... they're not learning at all. Nothing... has updated automatically... therefore these are not Agentic Experts."* (8:36) **Agent experts must learn on their own.**

**Retrieval.** Meta-agentics *act*. Why aren't they experts?

---

## Idea 6 — The pattern: **Act · Learn · Reuse** *(the one to memorize)*

**Hook.** Everything collapses to three steps. *[frame t1305 — the branded Act/Learn/Reuse graphic over a real expert prompt]*

**Picture.** A loop: **Act** (☀ take a useful action) → **Learn** (🧠 store new info) → **Reuse** (🔁 pull from the mental model next time) → back to Act.

**Worked example.** Watch which files supply which step (see Idea 9). The keyword is **useful** — and its honest twin: *"after your thorough search, there may be nothing to be done — this is perfectly acceptable."*

**Name it.** *"Act, learn, reuse. Act. First, our agents take a useful action. The keyword there is useful."* (21:41)

**Failure mode.** Building only Reuse + Learn and expecting compounding gains — without an **Act** step there's no useful action to learn from (that's the "partial expert" trap in Idea 9).

**Retrieval.** Three steps, and the keyword? What's the "perfectly acceptable" outcome of a learn pass?

---

## Idea 7 — The expertise file: anatomy of a mental model

**Hook.** "What's actually *in* one of these?" *[frame t2182 — the 677-line websocket file, collapsed to its spine]*

**Picture.** A YAML outline with exact `file:line` references, e.g. `overview → core_implementation → event_types → streaming_architecture → … → architecture_summary`.

**Worked example.** The database file's `session_state.websocketEventCount` entry (in the websocket file) records `lines: "78"`, `reset_on: connect (line 388), disconnect (line 409)`. Dan notes the database file has *"44 instances of specific line numbers"* — so the agent can jump straight to code and re-validate fast.

**Name it.** *"Give your agents a mental model by giving them an expertise file."* (16:08) Format is your choice — Dan likes YAML but says TOML/JSON/CSV/DB-JSONB all work; pick what's easiest for your agents to read.

**Failure mode.** Letting it grow forever. A hard `MAX_LINES: 1000` lives in the self-improve prompt and the agent enforces it on itself (`wc -l`, then trim least-critical). Dan stays under ~1000 lines.

**Retrieval.** What keeps an expertise file from bloating, and why does it carry exact line numbers?

---

## Idea 8 — The self-improve prompt: the **Learn** mechanism (and the golden rule)

**Hook.** How does a file "improve itself"? It doesn't — a prompt improves it. *[frame t1255 — self-improve.md workflow]*

**Picture.** A closed loop: `(git diff) → read current expertise → validate vs codebase → list discrepancies → update → enforce line limit → validate YAML compiles`.

**Worked example.** Run `/experts:database:self-improve`. The agent burns top-to-bottom, checks line count, compiles the YAML (`python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(...)"`), and reports discrepancies — or reports there was nothing to do and stops. Dan seeds **loosely** and lets the agent define its own structure ("it's their mental model, not yours").

**Name it (the golden rule).** *"We're not going to update the expertise file... Teach your agents how to directly update it so they can maintain it."* (37:00) → *"Build the system that builds the system. Do not work on the application layer. You're wasting your time."* (37:10)

**Failure mode.** Hand-editing the expertise file when it's wrong. It feels harmless, but it quietly restores manual memory maintenance — the exact problem experts remove — and never fixes the root cause: the **self-improve prompt**.

**Retrieval.** The mental model is wrong. What do you change, and what do you refuse to touch?

---

## Idea 9 — Partial vs complete expert: the **missing Act step**

**Hook.** Dan shows a *partial* expert first — on purpose.

**Picture.** A checklist per expert: `[Act] [Learn] [Reuse]`.

**Worked example.**
| | Database expert | WebSocket expert |
|---|---|---|
| **Reuse** | `question.md` (read expertise → validate → answer; **read-only**) | `plan.md` / `question.md` |
| **Learn** | `self-improve.md` | `self-improve.md` (run with `true` → reads the git diff) |
| **Act** | ❌ none — no prompt changes code | ✅ `build.md` edits real code |
| **Orchestration** | — | `plan_build_improve.md` chains all three *[frame t1598]* |

The database expert is *"completely acceptable"* — a fine partial. The websocket expert adds the Act step (build a session-based nav-bar WebSocket counter), completing the loop.

**Name it.** *"Now, where's our act step? We don't actually have any action prompts here. Nothing is changing."* (22:20) → the missing act = *"updating any code related to the database."*

**Failure mode.** Assuming an expert must always modify code. Read-only experts (Q&A over a mental model) are legitimate — they just run Reuse + Learn without Act.

**Retrieval.** Which step does the database expert lack, and what supplies it in the websocket expert?

---

## Idea 10 — Context delegation & "more compute = more confidence"

**Hook.** A complete expert runs a lot of tokens. How does the top agent not drown?

**Picture.** A conductor (top agent) firing three fresh musicians (sub-agents), each handed only what they need, handing back only a summary. *[frame t2019 — three Task blocks with token stats]*

**Worked example.** `plan_build_improve.md` spawns three `Task` sub-agents in sequence — **plan (81.8k tokens) → build (61.4k tokens, 41 tool uses) → self-improve** — each starting fresh, so the top agent's context stays protected; it just passes the plan into the builder and the git diff into self-improve. Separately, Dan fires the *same* websocket question at **three** experts to co-locate on the answer; websocket-3 fails — and that's the point.

**Name it.** *"Instead of having one agent answer something for you, have three, have five, have 10... more compute equals more confidence."* (25:00) Ties back to TAC-6: **one agent, one prompt, one purpose** — even inside a scaled workflow.

**Failure mode.** Reading parallel experts as waste. For high-stakes answers, redundancy surfaces evidence a single run misses; you compose the survivors.

**Retrieval.** Why isolate plan/build/self-improve into separate sub-agents? Why fire three experts at one question?

---

## Idea 11 — Product agent experts: per-user mental models + generative UI

**Hook.** Point the same pattern at *users* instead of code and you get a seed of a new product class. *[frames t2545 → t2588, a before/after]*

**Picture.** One expertise file **per user**: `{viewed_products, added_to_cart, checked_out}` → a prompt that streams UI components on the fly.

**Worked example (Nile).** New user, empty expertise → **generic** "Welcome to Nile." Dan searches "Nvidia DGX," adds to cart (an **Act**), returns → the agent **learned** and **reused**: "Welcome back! Based on your interest in AI workstations," streaming a personalized "Complete Your AI Workstation" carousel. The system prompt exposes dynamic vars (checked-out/added/viewed products) and static vars (`SECTIONS_RANGE 4-6`, `PRODUCTS_PER_SECTION_RANGE 6-12`); it's driven by the **Claude Agent SDK** (`agent_expert.py`), and Dan drops Opus→Haiku for speed on camera.

**Name it.** *"when they act, your agent learns, and then it reuses to enhance the experience... This is personalization to the max, especially when you combine that with generative UI."* (42:xx)

**Failure mode.** Mistaking this for a production recommendation engine. Dan is explicit: **it isn't** — agents are too slow for that today; study the *pattern in a UI*, and note the "UI hacks" (loading bars, streamed sections) needed to mask latency.

**Retrieval.** In Nile, what's the per-user mental model, and where do Act/Learn/Reuse show up in the shopping flow?

---

## Idea 12 — When to build an expert (and when NOT to)

**Hook.** The scary insight: build these in your *highest-stakes* code, not your safest.

**Picture.** A 2×2 — risk/complexity vs how-much-it-changes. Experts belong top-right; generic agents belong bottom-left.

**Worked example — build one for:** billing (Dan builds none without an expert; they've *"caught revenue changing details"*), security, the database, DevOps, tricky 3–4-way integrations, ML/data-science, APIs, and **data-types-kept-in-sync** across microservices (a great *first* expert — few files to reference). *"As the complexity, as the size of your codebase grows, the agent expert becomes more valuable."* (56:50)

**Don't build one when:** the problem doesn't evolve; the codebase is simple or brand-new (the model has seen its shape); or **you** don't have a mental model of the area — *"If you don't understand the problem, do not build an Agentic expert... It'll make your problems worse, not better."*

**Failure modes / trade-offs to expect (48:09–53:45):** *seeding* (start blank, let the agent define structure, rerun until it stops finding things), the *"another source of truth"* reflex (it's a mental model — invest in teaching your agents), *finite context* (max-line limit), *false expertise* (agents err like we do — expect it), *too-granular* expertise (a prompt-engineering fix: "prioritize actionable, high-value expertise over verbose documentation"), and *too many experts* (routers/reminders; habit: read the expertise file before working an area).

**Name it (the close).** *"Do you want a generalist working on your codebase that forgets every time they work? Or do you want an expert that remembers and learns from the work done?"* (61:29)

**Retrieval.** Name three build-it domains and one don't-build case. What's the risk of building an expert for a domain you don't understand?

|---|---|

# AH-5 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

Ordering rule: how much of the lesson collapses if this nugget is missing. **Tier 1** is the load-bearing idea; **Tier 2** is the working machinery you'll actually type; **Tier 3** is the framing that keeps you honest about *when* to reach for this.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. Agents forget, so they don't learn — that's the whole problem.**
Normal software improves with use; agents start cold every session. No prompt or context trick fixes this because it's *structural*. Agent experts fix it by **storing** what was learned.
*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds obvious, so they skip the consequence — everything else in the lesson exists only because of this.

**2. Agent expert = a normal agent in an Act → Learn → Reuse loop over a mental model.**
Not a smarter model, not a longer system prompt, not custom tools (the two demos have none). The magic is the loop + a persistent expertise file. *"One executes and forgets, the other executes and learns."*
*Test yourself:* define it in one sentence without the words "smart" or "model."

**3. The expertise file is a MENTAL MODEL, not a source of truth.**
The code is the only source of truth. The file is a fast, fuzzy index the agent **re-validates against the code every time** ("validate against the codebase" literally appears twice in the question prompt). Your own head works the same way.
*Say it Dan's way:* "This is not a source of truth. This is your agent's mental model."

**4. Act · Learn · Reuse — memorize the loop.**
**Act:** take a *useful* action. **Learn:** store it (the self-improve prompt updates the expertise file). **Reuse:** read the mental model first next time. If you keep one image from this lesson, keep the Act/Learn/Reuse graphic sitting on top of a real expert prompt.

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**5. Mechanically, an expert is a "self-improving template meta prompt."**
Decompose the mouthful: *meta prompt* (a prompt that builds prompts) + *template* (fixed purpose/structure) + *self-improving* (updates an isolated file for next time). That's it. If you understand meta prompts, you understand experts.

**6. Reuse is "read expertise → validate → answer." Never search blind.**
Watch the database question prompt: its first action is `Read(expertise.yaml)`, *then* it reads `models.py` and the migrations to confirm. Instant, no hunting. That first read is the entire differentiator.

**7. Learn is a prompt, not magic — and it's a closed loop.**
`self-improve.md`: (git diff) → read current expertise → validate vs code → list discrepancies → update → **enforce a hard line limit (wc -l, trim)** → **compile the YAML**. And it's allowed to find nothing: *"after your thorough search, there may be nothing to be done — this is perfectly acceptable."*

**8. The Act step is what separates a partial expert from a complete one.**
Database expert = Reuse + Learn, **no Act** (nothing changes) → a fine *partial* expert. WebSocket expert adds Act (a `build` step that edits code) → complete. `plan_build_improve.md` chains **plan (reuse) → build (act) → self-improve (learn)** as one one-shot prompt.

**9. Golden rule: never hand-edit the expertise file. Fix the self-improve prompt.**
See something wrong in the mental model? Don't open the file. Change the *learning rubric* so the agent produces the fix itself. *"Build the system that builds the system. Do not work on the application layer."* Editing the file by hand silently puts you back to manual memory maintenance.

**10. Delegate context; scale compute for confidence.**
`plan_build_improve` fires three **fresh sub-agents** so the top agent's context stays protected (plan ~81.8k tokens, build ~61.4k / 41 tools, then self-improve). Separately: fire the same question at 3–5 experts and compose the survivors — *"more compute equals more confidence"* (one may fail; one may find what others missed).

**11. Seed loosely; cap hard.**
Start from a **blank** expertise file and let the agent define the structure via self-improve; rerun until it stops finding new things. Then keep it under ~1000 lines with a `MAX_LINES` the agent enforces on itself.

**12. Meta-agentics are the atoms — but they're not experts.**
Meta prompt → new prompt, meta agent → new sub-agent, meta skill → new skill. They *act* but never *learn*. *"Every codebase must have meta agentics"* — just don't mistake them for experts.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you honest

**13. Build experts in your scariest code, not your safest.**
Billing, security, the database, gnarly integrations, types-in-sync across services. *"My Agentic Experts have caught revenue changing details."* The higher the risk/complexity and the more it grows, the more an expert is worth.

**14. Don't build one when there's nothing to learn — or when *you* can't judge it.**
Static problems, simple/brand-new codebases (the model has seen their shape), or domains where **you** lack a mental model → use a plain generic agent. Building an expert you can't evaluate makes things worse.

**15. Product experts are a *seed*, not a shipping recommendation engine.**
Nile shows Act/Learn/Reuse per user (viewed/added/checked-out → personalized generative UI). Dan is explicit: agents are too slow for real-time recommendations today; study the pattern, expect to hide latency with UI hacks.

**16. False expertise is permanent — design for it.**
Agents make the same kinds of mistakes we do (they're trained on us). Error rates fall as models improve and fact-checkers get better, but it never fully goes away. Treat a self-improve diff like a PR in high-stakes systems.

**17. Everything is still the core four.**
Skill, sub-agent, MCP server, custom system prompt — pick by ergonomics. Underneath, an expert is just **context, model, prompt, tools** with a little structure. Stay close to bare metal.

---

## Micro-quiz (close the book first)

1. Why is "agents forget" a *structural* problem, and what does an expert add to fix it?
2. Define an agent expert in one sentence. Which three files/steps make the loop?
3. Is the expertise file a source of truth? What is — and what does the expert do with the file first?
4. The database expert is "partial." Which step is missing, and what supplies it in the websocket expert?
5. The mental model is wrong. What do you change, and what do you refuse to touch — and why?
6. Why fire three experts at one question? Why isolate plan/build/self-improve into separate sub-agents?
7. Name two systems you'd build an expert for and one you wouldn't. What makes the "wouldn't" case a trap?

*(Answers live in extract.md — Ideas 1, 2/9, 3, 9, 8, 10, 12.)*

Database expert = Reuse + Learn, **no Act** (nothing changes) → a fine *partial* expert. WebSocket expert adds Act (a `build` step that edits code) → complete. `plan_build_improve.md` chains **plan (reuse) → build (act) → self-improve (learn)** as one one-shot prompt.

**9. Golden rule: never hand-edit the expertise file. Fix the self-improve prompt.**
See something wrong in the mental model? Don't open the file. Change the *learning rubric* so the agent produces the fix itself. *"Build the system that builds the system. Do not work on the application layer."* Editing the file by hand silently puts you back to manual memory maintenance.

**10. Delegate context; scale compute for confidence.**
`plan_build_improve` fires three **fresh sub-agents** so the top agent's context stays protected (plan ~81.8k tokens, build ~61.4k / 41 tools, then self-improve). Separately: fire the same question at 3–5 experts and compose the survivors — *"more compute equals more confidence"* (one may fail; one may find what others missed).

**11. Seed loosely; cap hard.**
Start from a **blank** expertise file and let the agent define the structure via self-improve; rerun until it stops finding new things. Then keep it under ~1000 lines with a `MAX_LINES` the agent enforces on itself.

**12. Meta-agentics are the atoms — but they're not experts.**
Meta prompt → new prompt, meta agent → new sub-agent, meta skill → new skill. They *act* but never *learn*. *"Every codebase must have meta agentics"* — just don't mistake them for experts.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you honest

**13. Build experts in your scariest code, not your safest.**
Billing, security, the database, gnarly integrations, types-in-sync across services. *"My Agentic Experts have caught revenue changing details."* The higher the risk/complexity and the more it grows, the more an expert is worth.

**14. Don't build one when there's nothing to learn — or when *you* can't judge it.**
Static problems, simple/brand-new codebases (the model has seen their shape), or domains where **you** lack a mental model → use a plain generic agent. Building an expert you can't evaluate makes things worse.

**15. Product experts are a *seed*, not a shipping recommendation engine.**
Nile shows Act/Learn/Reuse per user (viewed/added/checked-out → personalized generative UI). Dan is explicit: agents are too slow for real-time recommendations today; study the pattern, expect to hide latency with UI hacks.

**16. False expertise is permanent — design for it.**
Agents make the same kinds of mistakes we do (they're trained on us). Error rates fall as models improve and fact-checkers get better, but it never fully goes away. Treat a self-improve diff like a PR in high-stakes systems.

**17. Everything is still the core four.**
Skill, sub-agent, MCP server, custom system prompt — pick by ergonomics. Underneath, an expert is just **context, model, prompt, tools** with a little structure. Stay close to bare metal.

---

## Micro-quiz (close the book first)

1. Why is "agents forget" a *structural* problem, and what does an expert add to fix it?
2. Define an agent expert in one sentence. Which three files/steps make the loop?
3. Is the expertise file a source of truth? What is — and what does the expert do with the file first?
4. The database expert is "partial." Which step is missing, and what supplies it in the websocket expert?
5. The mental model is wrong. What do you change, and what do you refuse to touch — and why?
6. Why fire three experts at one question? Why isolate plan/build/self-improve into separate sub-agents?
7. Name two systems you'd build an expert for and one you wouldn't. What makes the "wouldn't" case a trap?

*(Answers live in extract.md — Ideas 1, 2/9, 3, 9, 8, 10, 12.)*

# AH-5 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)

Agent Experts ages well because it teaches a **pattern over primitives** (Act/Learn/Reuse over an expertise file, all reducing to the core four), and Dan repeatedly says to break the rules and use whatever abstraction fits. Six things have moved since recording. For each: what the course shows, current practice, and whether the book needs an overlay.

---

## 1. Agent memory: a detached expertise file vs Claude Code's memory features  ⟵ the design conversation to have

**Course era:** Dan deliberately rejects always-loaded **memory files** (CLAUDE.md-style) for experts because "expertise requires breaking rules when the time is right" and forced global context can't detach when it should. Instead he uses a **dedicated, topic-scoped, agent-maintained** expertise file loaded on demand by the expert prompt.
**Current:** Claude Code's memory surface has grown — CLAUDE.md imports/hierarchy, and an Anthropic **memory tool / pattern** for cross-session state. These make "give the agent memory" easier, but they don't decide *what shape* that memory should take.
**Book treatment:** overlay-as-contrast, not correction. Teach Dan's argument — **topic-scoped, self-maintained, on-demand** memory beats always-on memory for experts — then map it onto today's memory features so the reader chooses deliberately. Note: he explicitly says you *can* use memory files with auto-update if you like; he just prefers a detached file.
**Overlay:** best served by a memory/self-improving-agents video (see decision table #1 — ID needs sourcing).

## 2. Packaging: raw prompt-file expert → Agent Skills (and the Agent SDK)

**Course era:** experts are raw slash-command prompt files under `.claude/commands/experts/<domain>/` plus a YAML expertise file, orchestrated with in-Claude-Code primitives (`SlashCommand` inside `Task`, `TaskOutput`).
**Current:** **Agent Skills** (`SKILL.md` + progressive disclosure) are the first-class, discoverable, on-demand encoding — a natural home for an expert (a skill that loads its expertise file and a self-improve routine). Dan half-predicts this on camera (*"skills boil down to prompts"*), and the repo's **meta-skill already scaffolds Skills**. For production, the **Claude Agent SDK** (Python/TS) wraps Act/Learn/Reuse outside an interactive session — and the Nile product expert *already uses it* (`ClaudeSDKClient`, `@tool`, `create_sdk_mcp_server`).
**Book treatment:** teach the raw prompt-file expert first (pedagogically perfect — no magic), then show the same expert as a Skill and note the SDK path for non-interactive/production use.
**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**, pending ID re-verification).

## 3. Orchestration: slash-command chaining → SDK subagents/hooks

**Course era:** `plan_build_improve.md` chains three fresh sub-agents via the `Task` tool, each running a slash command; context is protected by spawning fresh agents.
**Current:** the same "isolate each step in a fresh subagent" idea is a supported SDK pattern (structured output, hooks, permission modes, subagents). The concept — **context delegation** — is unchanged; the machinery is richer and works headlessly.
**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the `Task`-chaining you see has a grown-up SDK form"); concept identical.
**Overlay:** none required.

## 4. Models & speed: course-era Claude 4.5 family, Opus→Haiku swap

**Course era:** on-screen model IDs are `claude-opus-4-5-20251101`, `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`, `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`; Dan drops Opus→Haiku live "just for speed."
**Current:** newer families (Opus 4.x → 5, etc.) change **nothing** about the pattern. "More compute = more confidence" and "as models improve, false-expertise error rates drop" are the durable claims; specific IDs are period detail.
**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected frames ("model IDs are period detail; the pattern is identical today").
**Overlay:** none.

## 5. False expertise → evaluation, drift-control, and review gates

**Course era:** Dan names **false expertise** as inherent ("I have false expertise... expect this") and predicts "great sophisticated models to fact check things," but the lesson's control is mostly the self-improve validation loop (line limit + YAML compile + validate-against-code).
**Current:** for high-stakes experts, teams add **evals**, periodic **re-seeding**, and **diff-review gates** on the expertise file — treat each self-improve output like a pull request, especially in billing/security. This is the missing playbook the book should supply.
**Book treatment:** "current practice" callout after the challenges section; frame the expertise diff as a reviewable artifact.
**Overlay:** none identified (topic-anchored; source if a good one exists).

## 6. Product/generative-UI experts: still latency-bound, more viable

**Course era:** the Nile per-user expert streams generated UI sections; Dan is explicit it's a **seed, not production** — agents too slow for real-time recommendations — and calls for "UI hacks" (loading bars, streamed sections) to mask latency.
**Current:** streaming component protocols, tool-driven UI, and faster small models make adaptive/generative UI more practical than at recording, but it remains latency-sensitive. Still an *emerging class*, not a ship-today recipe.
**Book treatment:** frame as "a class of product to watch/prototype," carry Dan's caveat forward verbatim.
**Overlay:** none required.

---

- The core thesis: agents forget → don't learn, and the fix is a **stored, self-maintained mental model**. More consensus now than at recording.
- **Act · Learn · Reuse** as the minimal anatomy of a learning agent.
- **Expertise file = mental model, not a source of truth**; the code is the only source of truth and the file is re-validated against it.
- **Never hand-edit the expertise file — fix the self-improve step.** ("Build the system that builds the system.")
- The **partial vs complete** distinction (the missing Act step).
- **Seeding loosely** + **hard line limits** + **expect false expertise**.
- **When-to / when-not** judgment (high-risk/complexity/error-rate/evolving vs static/simple/new/no-mental-model).
- **Everything reduces to the core four** — pick the abstraction (skill/subagent/MCP) by ergonomics.

The single best "current practice" upgrade to weave through this chapter is the **memory-vs-expertise-file** contrast (gap #1) and the **Skill/SDK packaging** (gap #2) — both are things Dan *gestures at himself*, so they read as "here's where this went," not "here's what Dan got wrong."
